### 2026-10-07

# Pre-registration

Pre-registered for the test window as `M0029-B70-RAW-FRAC` (dev trial #124, config digest `d4582ffd3518d62ba4f8e9d2dfc1679e680dfbee4790aec7307893af149e2059`, MAR 0.739747, DSR 0.930881 at N = 123; the bar it cleared is the one named in the pre-registration's gate line).

Pre-registration: `docs/lab/prereg/M0029.md`, written before any test number exists and committed before the look is spent (design §3). The test window is 2015-10-19..data end; `lab test M0029-B70-RAW-FRAC` spends the one look this configuration gets, and the database refuses a second (`UNIQUE(config_digest, window)`). No `trials` row was written here: a pre-registration is not a backtest and does not move the lab's N.


### 2026-10-07

## Dev run (1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16)

One version, the same 70/30 split M0021 pre-registered, in fractional shares. It grew **+13.5% a year** against SPY's +7.9%. Its worst fall was **18.2%**, under the 20% limit. It made 2.16 dollars of gains for every dollar of losses, over 2,786 trades. Its luck score was 0.931 against the 0.90 bar at N = 123: all conditions pass. It made a little more than the whole-share version (+12.6%) but fell further (18.2% vs 14.0%). So whole shares were quietly shaping the older history too: some slots stayed in cash, and cash softened the 1998 fall.

## The look at 2015-10-19 → 2026-10-06 (the lab's second test-window look)

**Test-failed, and that is final.** The book grew **+7.4% a year** (+118% in total) against **+13.6% a year** (+306%) for SPY with dividends. Its worst fall was **24.8%** (21.7% on month-end values, January 2022 to November 2023), over the 20% limit. It made 1.33 dollars of gains for every dollar of losses, barely above the 1.3 bar. It failed two of the five conditions: it did not beat SPY, and it fell too far.

This time the account size is not the excuse. On average 79% of the money was invested, more than on the dev window (62%). The picks were bought, and they lagged.

| year | this book | note |
|---|---|---|
| 2016 | +15.2% | |
| 2017 | +9.1% | |
| 2018 | +1.5% | |
| 2019 | +3.0% | SPY about +31%: out after the late-2018 fall, back in late, calm stocks lagged |
| 2020 | +12.6% | |
| 2021 | +18.0% | |
| 2022 | −9.6% | |
| 2023 | −5.2% | SPY about +26%: momentum's 2022 winners (energy, defensives) reversed as tech led |
| 2024 | +10.2% | SPY about +25% |
| 2025 | +10.0% | |
| 2026 (to Oct) | +24.3% | |

**Why.** The decade belonged to a handful of giant tech stocks. An equal-weight book of 40 names can't keep up with that by design. Its calm half held utilities and staples, which lagged badly. The momentum half was caught at the 2022–23 turn: it held last year's winners (energy, defensives) just as the market rotated back into tech. The 200-day filter took it out after the falls of late 2018, spring 2020 and 2022 and put it back in after the rebounds had started. That is the same cost the dev window showed in sideways markets.

**What it says about the paper books.** The momentum half is the residual-momentum engine the paper books RAW-FR and RMW-FR trade. This look is the lab's first sign of how that engine did after 2015. Without the calm half and without our filter it may have done differently, but it is the only clean evidence we have. Their month-by-month paper record against SPY is now the test to watch.

**My opinion:** the two-engine idea is not dead, but this pair is. Pairing momentum with calm stocks protected the old history's crashes (1998, 2000–02, 2008), while the last decade's risk was being *left behind* by a few giants, which neither engine owns. A partner that holds the market itself (an SPY core) would close that gap. The lab already tried a timed SPY core with a momentum satellite (P7a F9) and rejected it on the dev window, but that was before this lesson. The next blend should be an untimed SPY core plus a momentum satellite.

methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-07

## What we tried

M0029's look at 2016–2026 showed our books' recent risk is being *left behind* by a few giant companies, not crashing. This method holds the market itself (SPY) as the core, so those leaders are always owned, and puts the rest in the lab's best stock picker, the residual-momentum top 20 (M0007-N20-RAW's book). Everything is in fractional shares, the way paper would trade it. Three versions were fixed before any result:

| version | core | split | CAGR (yearly growth) | worst fall | gains vs losses | Sharpe (steadiness) | luck score (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C70T | SPY, out below its 200-day average | 70 / 30 | +11.5% | 18.8% | 3.70x | 0.86 | 0.838 |
| C50T | SPY, out below its 200-day average | 50 / 50 | **+12.7%** | 18.6% | 2.79x | 0.89 | **0.873** |
| C50A | SPY always held | 50 / 50 | +11.9% | 34.0% | 2.12x | 0.77 | 0.732 |
| *SPY with dividends* | | | *+7.9%* | *~55%* | | | |
| *F9 (timed SPY 70 + plain momentum 30, whole shares)* | | | *+12.2%* | *19.2%* | *4.28x* | *0.87* | *—* |

Window: 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16 (dev only), about 1,600 trades each.

**None is eligible.** All three beat SPY with dividends, have well over 100 trades, and make far more in gains than in losses. Both filtered versions keep the worst fall under the 20% limit (18.6–18.8%). They fail only the **luck test**. That test asks whether a result is real or just the best of many tries, judged against N = 126, every dev trial the lab has run, with a bar of DSR ≥ 0.90 (the owner's setting since 2026-10-07). C50T scored 0.873, 0.027 short. C70T scored 0.838. The always-on core also broke the 20% limit (34.0%) in 2008, as predicted.

## When it hurt

Both filtered versions had their worst fall in the summer-1998 shock: on month-end values 16–17% from June to August 1998, and 18.6–18.8% on daily values. The SPY filter reacts too slowly to a six-week crash, and the momentum half fell harder than the market. The 2001, 2002 and 2008 bear markets are flat years (0%), because the filter took everything to cash. The worst calendar year is 2015 (−4 to −5%). The always-on core lost 30.7% from October 2007 to February 2009 (−20% in 2008).

## Why

- **The core does what it was meant to.** In the strong market years the book keeps up with or beats SPY: 1999 +35%, 2003 +33%, 2013 +39% (C50T). The equal-weight calm-stock pairing could not do that in 2016–2026.
- **But the core adds return without adding steadiness.** SPY under a 200-day filter is roughly SPY's return with the bear markets cut out. Its ups and downs move with the momentum half's (both are the US stock market), so the blend is not much steadier than momentum alone (Sharpe 0.89 vs 0.94). The calm-stock pairing reached a Sharpe of 1.01 because calm stocks fell at *different* times. Steadiness is what the luck test rewards, so the core gives back luck score.
- **The filter matters.** Without it, half the money rode SPY down in 2008, and the worst fall nearly doubled (34% vs 18.6%) for less return.

## Hypothesis vs result

- **C70T.** Predicted near F9's +12% with a worst fall under 20% and a luck score above 0.90. Got +11.5%, 18.8% and 0.838. **Return and worst fall held, luck missed.** The residual-momentum satellite did *not* beat F9's plain-momentum satellite here.
- **C50T.** Predicted near +13% at a similar worst fall with luck above 0.90. Got +12.7%, 18.6% and 0.873. **Return and worst fall held, luck missed.**
- **C50A.** Predicted to break the 20% limit in 2008. It did (34.0%). **Held.**
- **Expected failure.** Dilution toward SPY with luck short of 0.90 happened for both filtered versions, more for 70/30. The "near the limit" worst fall happened too (18.6%).

## My opinion

This is the right direction for the decade we actually live in, but it is not yet a result. A core-plus-satellite book keeps up in leader-driven markets, which no earlier book could. Its weakness is steadiness, and the fix is a satellite that is steadier than raw momentum, not a different core split. I would try the 50/50 timed core with the *braked* residual-momentum book as the satellite: M0022's weekly volatility brake, the lab's steadiest single book (on paper as RMW-FR). That attacks exactly the luck score and the 1998 shock. I would not try more splits of this pair. A 60/40 or 40/60 is a dial turned after seeing results, and it would cost N for a few hundredths of luck score.

The variants this unblocks:

- `M0030-C50T`: DSR 0.9590 at N = 28, against DSR >= 0.90.

The *set* of five P7a D8 conditions did not change, and `owner inputs` -- the one that is a property of the candidate rather than of a number -- was carried from the record untouched. Status moves `rejected` -> `dev-eligible`.

methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-08

**What this is.** The same idea as its parent — rank stocks on how much they moved *after* taking
out the part the whole market explains, hold the best twenty, equal money in each, and stand aside
when the market itself is below its 200-day average — run the way you actually trade it. Three
things changed and nothing else did:

1. **Fractional shares.** Every one of the twenty slots is actually bought. In the old run the
   account started at 20 million rupiah, so a slot was worth twenty to seventy dollars, and whole
   shares of most big index names cost more than that. Those picks were silently skipped and their
   money sat in cash doing nothing.
2. **Gotrade's real fees.** The fee schedule fitted to your own order receipts — a trading fee with
   a ten-cent floor, a small regulatory fee, and 11% tax on both — instead of the lab's old
   pretend flat rate of a tenth of a percent a trade.
3. **Your real funding.** 5 million rupiah on the 25th of every month, on top of the opening
   account. Over the window that is 237 deposits and about 148,000 dollars paid in. It is judged
   against putting those exact same deposits, on those exact same days, into the market instead.

**What your money actually earned: 13.7% a year. The same deposits put into the market instead
earned 7.2% a year.** That is the headline, and it is the only fair comparison a funded run has:
both sides got the same money on the same days, so neither gets credit for timing the deposits.
Six and a half points a year, every year, for twenty years, on money that kept arriving.

**The big total number on this page is not a return.** This run shows a total of +55,492% and a
yearly figure of +37.6%. Almost all of that is your own deposits piling up — 148,000 dollars paid
in is counted as if it were 148,000 dollars made. The engine leaves those two figures alone on
purpose, because older results on the site depend on them being the recorded shape of the curve,
and it puts the honest number — the 13.7% above — beside them. Do not read the +37.6% as
performance, and never compare it to the parent's +15.0%.

**What the realism cost.** Measuring the fee change on its own first (the cost report run before
this method was registered), the parent's best variant went from +14.2% a year on pretend fees to
+12.8% on Gotrade's real ones. Fees went from eating about one twentieth of the gross trading
profit to about one sixth. That is the price of trading for real, and this book survives it easily
because it is slow: roughly eighty trades a year, not eighty a week.

Fractional shares then pushed in the other direction. The money invested went from about 62% of the
account to **69%** — seven more points of your money actually working, because no pick gets skipped
for being too expensive for its slot any more. That is where the 13.7% comes from: it is slightly
*better* than the 12.8% the fees alone implied, and the extra is the cash that used to sit idle.

**What it misses.** One condition, and only just: the worst fall. Measured day by day the account
dropped **20.6%** from a peak, which is about six tenths of a point over the limit. Everything else
clears: gains against losses came in at 1.98 (comfortably above the minimum), and the luck score —
how likely the result is real rather than a fluke after this many distinct ideas tried — came in at
0.939, which clears the bar the lab is using today. The worst stretch was the summer of 1998, when
Russia defaulted and a large hedge fund blew up; the worst calendar year was 2015, down 4.1%.

**Two numbers you might expect to be flattered by the deposits, and are not.** When money keeps
arriving, an account naturally looks safer than the strategy is — a deposit refills the hole, so the
fall looks shallower — and the day a deposit lands looks like an enormous winning day, which would
inflate the luck score. The engine fixes both, deliberately. The fall is measured on the path a
single unchanging dollar would have traced, not on the raw balance; and the deposit is divided out
of the day it lands on before any daily figure is worked out. On the test fixture the unfixed
version reported a luck-relevant quality ten times too good. So the 20.6% and the 0.939 here are
real. In fact the fall came out **deeper** than the parent's, not shallower — 20.6% against 19.3%
for the same variant at the same fees without deposits — which is exactly what more money invested
should do.

**Did the hypothesis hold?** Yes, on the question it was registered to answer. I predicted the
money-weighted return would still beat a deposit-matched market because the book trades too slowly
for a ten-cent fee floor to eat a four-and-a-half point margin, and that fractional fills would
remove cash drag. Both happened: 13.7% against 7.2%, with exposure up seven points.

**Did the expected failure happen?** No, and I was wrong about both halves of it. I expected the
monthly deposits to hand the comparison to the market, because this book sits in cash through
2000-02 and 2008-09 — precisely when a monthly buyer's new money buys cheapest. It did not: being
out of those two crashes turned out to protect the arriving money more than it cost it. I also
expected the ten-cent fee floor to bite on small early orders and drag the return-per-unit-of-fall
below the 0.66 the cost report measured. It came in at exactly 0.66. I was wrong about the
direction of the deposit effect on the worst fall too — I expected it to read shallower and it read
deeper, because the engine refuses to let deposits soften it.

**Why it works, in one line.** Stripping the market's own move out of the ranking leaves the part of
a stock's run that is actually about that stock, and that part keeps going without carrying the
market-crash risk the plain version carries. Add real fees and it still works, because the method
holds names for a month at a time rather than churning. Add fractional shares and it works slightly
better, because none of your money has to sit out.

**My opinion:** this direction deserves more trials, and it is now the strongest honest result in the
lab. It is not a fluke of pretend fees — that was the whole question, and the answer is no. It is
also not ready to trade: it fails the fall limit, and it fails it by so little that a modest brake
should close the gap. Its sibling already showed what that brake costs on this exact book: scaling
the position size down to a volatility target took the plain momentum version from a 22.2% fall to
12.9%, at roughly four fifths of a point of yearly return per point of fall removed. Six tenths of a
point of fall, bought at that rate, costs about half a point of yearly return — which would still
leave your money earning over 13% a year against the market's 7.2%. That is the next thing to run,
and I have queued it. Do not spend the test-window look on this version: fix the fall first, because
a method that fails a go-live condition on dev has nothing to prove on the test window.
methods.verdict: Real fees and fractional shares do not break this book: your money earned 13.7% a year against 7.2% for the same deposits put into the market, with more of it invested than before. It fails only the fall limit, and only by about half a point.

methods.name: The real-fee fractional residual book under an own-volatility brake
methods.sourceRef: M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT + M0011's own-volatility overlay (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015), on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, funded monthly
methods.hypothesis: M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT is the lab's first honest real-fee funded result and fails exactly one go-live condition: a 20.6% worst fall, about six tenths of a point over the 20% limit, with its luck score (0.939 at N=29) and gains-to-losses (1.98) both clear and your money earning +13.7% a year against +7.2% for the same deposits put into SPY TR. This method buys that six tenths of a point down with the cheapest brake that will do it, rather than the brake its sibling happened to test. Scaling every weight by min(1, target_vol / the target basket's own annualized volatility) is the overlay M0011 already measured on this exact ranking, and it measured the price too: 15.0% -> 10.8% a year buying 19.6% -> 14.1% worst fall, about 0.76 points of yearly return per point of fall removed. At that rate the six tenths of a point actually needed costs under half a point of yearly return -- but only if the brake is set to remove six tenths, not five points. So the dial is spanned, light end first. I expect TV20-N21 to win: a 20% volatility target barely binds in a calm market and clamps hard in a crash, which is where the 20.6% fall was made, so it should land near a 18-19% fall while giving up well under a point of yearly return -- a money-weighted return around 12.8-13.3% a year against the same deposit-matched SPY's 7.2%, which would be the widest honest margin in the lab and the first configuration to break no go-live condition at real fees. TV22-N21 is the control from above: if it also lands under 20% then the brake barely had to engage at all and the fall was made on a handful of days. TV18-N21 is the first fallback if the light end misses. The two TV14 anchors are not expected to win; they are there so the result is comparable with M0011's recorded ladder, and N21 should beat N63 on both return and fall exactly as it did there. The brake also has to survive a fee schedule it never faced: rescaling weights every month places resize trades the unscaled book does not, so trades should rise above M0032's 1,607 and the fee drag with them, which is the one way a light brake can cost more than the arithmetic says.
methods.expectedFailure: The brake does not bind where the fall was made, so the whole ladder either costs return without buying fall, or buys fall only by braking so hard that the return goes with it. M0032's worst fall is a funded-book fall, and the engine refuses to let deposits soften it, so it may well be a fast shock -- 1998, or the first weeks of 2008 -- that hit a book whose trailing volatility was still low going in. A min(1, target/realized) scale reads the past, so on a fall that arrives faster than the estimate the light targets sit at scale 1.0 and change nothing: TV22 and TV20 would come back at 20.5-20.6% with the return intact and nothing bought, and only TV14 would clear the limit, at the 3-4 points of yearly return the idea was written to avoid paying. That outcome is still worth the look, because it says the fall is a timing problem rather than a sizing problem and points at a drawdown brake on the book itself (M0009) instead. The second way it fails is the fee schedule: a 20-name book funded 5,000,000 IDR a month places small orders, and a brake that moves every weight a little every month turns 20 holds into 20 resizes, each paying a 0.10 USD floor on a slice that may be worth 30 dollars. If that lifts the trade count far above 1,607, the fee drag could take more yearly return than the brake saves in fall, leaving every variant worse than the unbraked parent on return per unit of fall.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

**What this is.** Your best honest book so far — rank stocks on how much they moved *after* taking
out the part the whole market explains, hold the best twenty in equal amounts, stand aside when
the market is below its 200-day average — with one thing added: a brake on position size. Each
month the book measures how jumpy its own twenty picks have been lately, and if they are jumpier
than a chosen target it buys less of each and leaves the rest in cash. Five brake settings were
fixed in advance, from very light to quite heavy, plus two settings copied from an earlier method
so the results stay comparable. Everything else is identical to the previous run: fractional
shares, Gotrade's real fees, and your real 5 million rupiah on the 25th of every month.

**Why there are five settings and not the one that was planned.** The queued idea said to run one
brake setting, copied from the earlier method that used this overlay. Reading that method's own
recorded results before writing the code said that was the wrong single choice, twice over, so I
changed it and wrote down why. First, the earlier method had tested the same brake on two
different measurement windows and the faster one was better on *both* counts — more return and a
shallower fall. The idea had reserved the loser. Second, and more important: the previous run
missed the fall limit by about six tenths of a point, and every brake setting that method had
tested removes four to five points of fall. Buying five points when you need six tenths means
paying for something you do not want. So I spanned the dial instead of guessing a point on it.
Nobody was asked; this is written here as the record.

**The headline.** Four of the five settings pass every one of your go-live rules. The best of
them, by the lab's own ranking, is the lightest brake:

| brake | your money earned | same deposits into SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | invested |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no brake (previous run) | +13.7%/yr | +7.2%/yr | 20.65% | 1.98 | 69.4% |
| lightest | +12.5%/yr | +7.2%/yr | **19.98%** | 1.94 | 66.0% |
| light | +12.2%/yr | +7.2%/yr | **20.00%** | 1.94 | 64.7% |
| medium | +11.6%/yr | +7.2%/yr | **19.94%** | 1.90 | 63.0% |
| heavy (fast window) | +9.8%/yr | +7.2%/yr | 16.39% | 1.82 | 56.5% |
| heavy (slow window) | +8.8%/yr | +7.2%/yr | 19.43% | 1.79 | 54.4% |

**Now read the three bold numbers again, because they are the whole story.** The limit is 20%.
The three light settings came in at 19.98%, 20.00% and 19.94%. The middle one is 19.9997% — it
clears your rule by three ten-thousandths of a percentage point. That is not a method passing a
test. That is a coin landing on its edge. One different fill, one different day's price, and it
fails. I am recording these as passes because they are passes and the gate is not mine to move,
but nobody should read them as a method that solved the problem.

**Why they are all stuck at the same number.** Look down the "invested" column: the brake really
is working, cutting the book from 69% invested to 66%, 65%, 63%. Real money is being held back.
And yet the worst fall barely moves — 20.65% down to 19.9%, and then it just sits there no matter
how much more you brake, until suddenly at the heavy setting it drops to 16.4%. Something is
clearly not being touched.

It is the summer of 1998. That is the worst fall in every single version, and it is a fast one:
the book peaked at the end of June and bottomed at the end of August. The brake looks *backwards*
at how jumpy the picks have been over the past month. Markets were calm going into that summer,
so the brake measured calm, decided no braking was needed, and was switched fully off on the way
in. It only woke up afterwards — once the fall had already happened and the picks were visibly
jumpy — which is exactly when the rebound comes. So the light settings take none of the fall and
some of the recovery. That is the worst possible half of the trade.

There is a fingerprint in the numbers that confirms it. As the brake tightens, the book's returns
get *more* lopsided to the downside, not less: the lopsidedness reading goes from −0.32 with no
brake to −0.48, −0.54, −0.59. A brake that genuinely protected you would make that number less
negative. This one makes it worse, because it is reliably absent for the falls and reliably
present for the recoveries.

**What the brake actually costs, which is far more than advertised.** The earlier method's results
suggested a rate of about 0.76 points of yearly return given up per point of fall removed. That
was measured across a big move, and I assumed it held for a small one. It does not. Going from no
brake to the lightest brake costs 1.2 points of yearly return and buys 0.67 points of fall — a
rate of 1.8, more than twice as expensive as assumed. The heavy fast setting costs 3.9 points and
buys 4.3, a rate of 0.9. So the light end of the dial is the *worst* deal on offer, not the
cheapest, because that is the end where the brake is paying for protection it does not deliver.

**The cleanest way to say it:** measured as return per unit of fall, every single brake setting is
worse than no brake at all — 0.66 with no brake, against 0.62, 0.61, 0.60, 0.58 and 0.45 with one.
The brake does not improve this book. It drags one number under one line, and charges more for
that than the line is worth.

**The luck score.** 0.938 when it ran, against your bar of 0.90, re-judged to 0.941 as other
methods finished today. In plain words: after 30 distinct methods had been tried in this lab, the
question is whether a result this good could be the best of 30 tries by chance alone. The answer
is that there is roughly a 94% chance it is real rather than luck, which clears the 90% bar you
set on 7 October. The number of tries and the bar are both read off the lab's own status; neither
is mine to set. Worth knowing: the heavy slow setting is the one failure here, and it failed on
exactly this — 0.849, below 0.90.

**Worst year.** 2015, down 4.1%, the same in every version — the brake does not help there either.
The worst fall, as above, is the summer of 1998 in all six.

**Did the hypothesis hold?** Half, and the useful half is the half that broke. I predicted the
light settings would land near an 18–19% fall and earn 12.8–13.3% a year. The earnings prediction
was right — 12.5% against the market's 7.2%, the widest honest margin the lab has. The fall
prediction was wrong, and wrong for the reason that matters: I said a light brake "barely binds in
a calm market and clamps hard in a crash". It does the opposite. It cannot clamp in a crash,
because it only learns there is a crash from the crash.

**Did the expected failure happen?** Yes, almost word for word, which is the one comfort here. I
wrote beforehand that the fall "may well be a fast shock — 1998, or the first weeks of 2008 — that
hit a book whose trailing volatility was still low going in", and that the light targets would
"sit at scale 1.0 and change nothing". It was 1998, and they very nearly did change nothing. I
also wrote that this outcome "says the fall is a timing problem rather than a sizing problem", and
that is now the finding. The other predicted failure — that rescaling every month would pile up
fees — did not happen at all: the trade count is 1,607 in every version, identical to the unbraked
run, because the book already resizes monthly. The brake changes how big the trades are, not how
many. Fees were never the issue.

**Comparison with the earlier method that used this overlay.** That one ran at the lab's old
pretend fee of a tenth of a percent, so comparing against its recorded numbers would let the fees
decide the answer. Re-run at Gotrade's real fees instead, its best version made +8.2% a year
against the market's +7.9% — a margin of three tenths of a point, where the pretend-fee version
had shown two full points. Real fees had quietly eaten nearly the whole edge, and it was only
46.4% invested, because whole shares at a small account size meant picks it chose were never
actually bought. The same brake setting here, in fractional shares on your monthly deposits, is
56.5% invested and earns 9.8% against 7.2% — a margin of 2.6 points. Ten extra points of your
money actually in the market turned a rounding error back into a real edge. That is a genuine
finding and it belongs to fractional shares, not to the brake.

**One honest caveat on my own arithmetic.** The cost report noted that re-running the earlier
method today does not reproduce the numbers in its own recorded row (+545% re-run against +660%
recorded) — the engine or the data has changed since. My pre-registered reasoning quoted those
recorded numbers. The conclusions above are drawn from runs made today against each other, which
is the valid comparison, but the "0.76 points per point" figure I wrote into the hypothesis came
from a row that today's engine would not produce. That is a second reason it mispredicted.

**My opinion:** this direction is finished, and I would not spend the one test-window look on it.
Not because the result is bad — 12.5% a year against 7.2% is the widest honest margin in the lab —
but because the only thing standing between this method and failure is three ten-thousandths of a
percentage point, on a fall that the brake demonstrably never touched. Four of your four previous
test-window looks failed, and every one of them failed on the drawdown rule. Sending a fifth one
whose dev-window margin is literally zero is walking into the same wall with the same blindfold.

There is a sharper problem underneath. The lab's promotion step picks a method's best version by
return-per-unit-of-fall, and that ranking picks the lightest brake (0.62) over the heavy fast one
(0.60) — a gap of two hundredths, well inside noise. But those two are not remotely equal in
safety: one clears your fall limit by 0.02 points and the other by 3.6. If this method is promoted
at all, the machinery will automatically spend your irreplaceable look on the fragile one. I have
journalled that as something to fix; it is not something I can override, because the promotion
command takes a method and chooses the version itself.

What I would do instead, and what I have queued: attack the actual mechanism. The fall is fast and
arrives in calm weather, so a brake that reads the past month cannot see it, and no amount of
tuning that brake will change this — this run tested five settings and all five failed the same
way. What can see it is something that reacts to the market's own fast move within days rather
than to the book's trailing jumpiness: the fast crash gate this lab already has. Pairing that with
this book, at real fees in fractional shares, is the next trial, and it is aimed at the one
episode that has set the worst fall in every residual-momentum run on record. I have also queued
the book's-own-drawdown brake, which cuts exposure when the account itself falls — it responds to
the loss rather than predicting it, which is the right shape for a shock you cannot forecast.
methods.verdict: Four of five brake settings clear every rule and your money earns 12.5% a year against 7.2% for the same deposits put into the market - but the three that keep the return pass the 20% fall limit by as little as three ten-thousandths of a point, because the fall is the fast summer of 1998 and a brake that reads the past month is switched off on the way in and on during the recovery.

methods.name: Size the picks by how big they trade, not equally: a size tilt inside the real-fee residual book
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT, re-weighted; lab insight 58's first recommendation; Russell 1000 Equal Weight vs its cap-weighted parent, Q4 2014 - Q1 2025
methods.hypothesis: Equal weights inside the top-20 are an unstated bet that the typical pick keeps up with the cap-weighted index the book is judged against, and insight 58 measured that the bet has been losing since late 2023: on a constant-coverage breadth reading the trailing three-year mean of the equal-weight-minus-cap spread peaked at +0.68% a month in December 2025, above the dot-com peak of +0.53%, where 1996-2015 cleared +0.17% in only 6 of 202 three-year windows. Published numbers agree -- the Russell 1000 Equal Weight index trailed its cap-weighted parent by roughly 3.9 points a year from Q4 2014 to Q1 2025. This method keeps M0032's ranking and execution exactly -- top-20 raw cumulative residual momentum, F4's screen, the SPY-200 trend gate, monthly, fractional shares at Gotrade's measured fees, funded 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th of each month -- and moves one dial: how the twenty slots are sized. The dial reads the 20-day mean of close times volume, which F4 already computes for every eligible name, NOT point-in-time market capitalisation: EDGAR's XBRL facts begin in 2009 and the dev window opens in 1996, so a book that needed a filed share count would hold nothing for thirteen of twenty years and would measure the SEC's filing mandate instead of the idea. Measured over the 69 month-end dates from 2010-01-29 to 2015-09-30 where both exist, trading size and market value rank the eligible set alike at a Spearman correlation of 0.686 on average and the chosen top-20 at 0.539, with 90% of the top-20 carrying a filed share count, and the two size-proportional books put about 35-40% of their money on different names (mean total-variation weight distance 0.400). Trading size is therefore a cousin of market value, not a stand-in for it, and this is a size-tilt trial honestly labelled. I expect the dev window to say the large tilt costs return: 1996-2015 is the era in which the typical stock did keep up, so the honest reading of a loss on dev is the size of an insurance premium against a regime the dev window does not contain. What is really being measured is how big that premium is, and whether leaning on the larger names shrinks the worst fall -- M0032 missed the 20% limit by six tenths of a point -- enough to buy some of it back. Equal weighting is the centre of this dial, not its end, so the inverse tilt is run too: if leaning small also beats equal, the dial is noise and the premium is not worth paying.
methods.expectedFailure: The size tilt does nothing measurable in either direction, because the universe is already the S&P 500 union the Nasdaq-100 and the trend-gated momentum screen keeps cutting it down to twenty large, liquid names whose trading sizes span perhaps one order of magnitude -- too narrow a spread for a weight tilt to move a twenty-year result by more than noise, and far narrower than the spread an all-cap equal-weight index runs against its parent. The second way it fails is the opposite and worse: the unconstrained size tilt concentrates. A single mega-cap can take 25-35% of a twenty-name book weighted by trading volume, which turns a diversified momentum book into a bet on one or two names, pushes the worst fall further past the 20% limit rather than back inside it, and makes the capped variant the only one that could ever be promoted. The third way, and the one that would make the whole direction a dead end, is that the inverse tilt wins too: both sides beating the control would mean the extra turnover of re-weighting is being paid back by nothing but noise, and the dial should be left where it is.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

**What this tested.** The picking stayed exactly as it is in the book you already know — rank
stocks on how much they rose beyond what the whole market explains, hold the best twenty, stand
aside whenever the market itself is below its 200-day average, rebalance monthly, buy fractional
shares, pay Gotrade's real fees, add 5 million rupiah on the 25th of every month. One dial moved:
**how much money goes into each of the twenty slots.** Today every slot gets the same. The
question was whether leaning toward the bigger names instead would help — because a book that
spreads its money evenly is quietly betting that its average pick keeps up with an index that
does *not* spread evenly, and the lab's own breadth work (journal entry 58) found that bet has
been losing badly since late 2023.

Five versions ran, so the dial could be read in both directions rather than only the one the idea
hoped for:

| Version | Money earned a year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Return per unit of fall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Even slots (the control) | **+13.7%** | 20.6% | 1.98 | 0.66 |
| Lean fully toward the big | **+15.0%** | **28.8%** | 2.19 | 0.52 |
| Lean half-way toward the big | +13.8% | 21.8% | 2.05 | 0.64 |
| Lean big, capped at 10% a name | **+12.0%** | 24.7% | 1.90 | 0.48 |
| Lean toward the *small* | **+14.0%** | **20.6%** | 1.95 | **0.68** |

The same deposits put into the market instead earned **+7.2% a year**. Every version beat that
comfortably. Every version also failed the same single condition — the worst fall must stay under
20% — so the method is rejected. Nothing here is promotable.

**The control proves the test was clean.** The even-slots version came back identical to M0032 on
every recorded number: same 1,607 trades, same 20.6% worst fall, same 1.98 gains-to-losses, same
69.4% of the money invested, same 0.66 return-per-fall. That is exactly what it should be — it is
M0032's configuration run through the new code — and it means every difference the other four
show is the money-sizing and nothing else. No fee change, no data change, no picking change.

**The answer is the opposite of the question, and it is not close.** Leaning toward the big names
made the book *worse*, and leaning toward the small ones made it slightly better. Reading the
dial from small to big, return-per-fall goes 0.68 → 0.66 → 0.64 → 0.52. That is not noise
scattered around the control; it slopes one way.

**Why: trading volume is not a size measure, it is a crowding measure.** The size dial here reads
how much money changes hands in a stock over 20 days, because that is the only size figure the
lab holds back to 1993 (more on that below). Inside a twenty-name momentum book that figure is
wildly lopsided — measured over 170 rebalances, the most-traded pick trades about **13 times**
the typical pick's volume, and in the worst month **61 times**. So "weight by trading size" does
not produce a gentle lean. It produces a one-stock book:

- **31 December 1999:** Qualcomm got **61% of the entire account.** The other nineteen names
  shared the rest.
- **31 March 2000:** Cisco 37% and Qualcomm 22% — nearly three-fifths of the money in two names,
  at the exact top of the dot-com bubble.
- **30 June 2014:** Apple 49% and Meta 26% — three-quarters in two names.

Across all 170 rebalances the big-lean version put an average of **27% of the account in a single
stock**, and behaved like a book of 8.6 names rather than 20. That is the whole story of the 28.8%
fall: its deepest slide ran from the last day of 1999 to the end of May 2000, while all the other
versions had their worst moment back in the 1998 Russia crisis. The big-lean book did not merely
drift into the dot-com crash — the dial *steered it there*, because in a momentum book the stock
everybody is trading hardest is by definition the most crowded trade, and that is where it put
the money, at maximum size, right before it broke.

**The capped version is the most useful failure of the five.** Putting a 10% ceiling on any one
name sounds like the obvious fix, and it came last: the **worst return of the group (+12.0%)** and
still a 24.7% fall. Capping kept the crowding — the money shoved off the biggest name just moved
to the second, third and fourth most crowded ones — while throwing away the only thing crowding
ever paid for, which was Qualcomm's 1999 run and Apple's 2014 run. It bought none of the safety
and sold all of the upside. A ceiling does not undo a bad weighting rule; it only makes it
cheaper and duller.

**The small-lean version is the one quiet positive.** It earned **+14.0% a year against the
control's +13.7%**, with the worst fall *fractionally smaller* (20.62% against 20.65%), the best
steadiness of the five, and the highest luck score. It is the least concentrated of them all —
no name above 12.5% ever, effectively 17 of the 20 names genuinely working. It is a de-crowding
rule: systematically underweight whatever the market is most excited about. The gain is real but
small — three tenths of a point a year — and it costs about 5% more trading to keep the weights
where they belong. It does not fix the drawdown, which is the only condition this family keeps
failing.

**Luck.** The lab has now tried **32 distinct methods**, and each result is discounted for that:
the more things you try, the more likely the best one is a fluke. The bar is a luck score of
**0.90 or better** — the owner's setting since 2026-10-07. The small-lean version scored **0.962**
and the control **0.944**, both clear. The two leaning big did not: 0.893 and 0.826. So on top of
their worse numbers, the big-lean versions are also the ones most likely to be noise. Note the
control's own score moved from 0.939 to 0.944 purely because the lab's method count moved from 29
to 32 — the score is relative to how hard the lab has been searching, not just to the result.

**Did the hypothesis hold? No — and I said the wrong thing would go wrong.** I predicted the big
lean would cost return and might buy back some of the drawdown. It did the reverse: it *made* the
most return (+15.0%) and *blew out* the drawdown (28.8%). I also guessed the trading sizes inside
the top twenty would span "perhaps one order of magnitude" and therefore barely matter. They span
closer to two, and they mattered enormously. The one prediction that did land was the second
failure mode written down before the run: "a single mega-cap can take 25-35% of the book... and
makes the capped variant the only one that could ever be promoted." The concentration arrived
even worse than that (up to 61%), and the capped variant then failed too, so even that escape
hatch is shut.

**An honest limit on what this proves, stated before the run and confirmed by it.** The idea
asked for a tilt by *market value* — company size. This tested a tilt by *trading volume*. Those
are not the same thing, and the lab cannot test the first one: the SEC filing data that carries
share counts begins in 2009, and this window opens in 1996, so a book needing real share counts
would have sat in cash for thirteen of twenty years. Before running, I measured how close a cousin
volume is to value over the 2010–2015 stretch where both exist: they rank the candidate list alike
about 0.69 of the way (1.0 would be identical, 0 would be unrelated), and the two weightings put
about 35–40% of the money on different names. So this result says something firm about leaning on
*crowding*, and nothing firm about leaning on *company size*. That question is still open and is
queued as its own idea.

**But the cap question may be dead on arrival too, and that is worth knowing now.** Out of
curiosity I measured what a real market-value weighting would have done to this book over
2010–2015, and it is *more* concentrated, not less: an average of **36% in one stock** and
effectively under seven names. The premise underneath the whole idea — "weight like the index and
the book moves toward the index" — turns out to be false at book scale. A cap-weighted index is
spread out because it holds five hundred names and its biggest is about 4% of it. A cap-weighted
*pick of twenty* is a bet on one company. Any rule that hands out money in proportion to a
lopsided quantity inside a small book is a concentration rule wearing a diversification costume.

**One thing I found by accident that matters more than this method.** While checking the above I
confirmed the lab's price history is back-adjusted for splits that happened *later* — Apple's
close on 16 October 2015 is stored as 27.76 where the real price that day was 111.04, because
Apple split four-for-one in 2020. That is correct and normal for returns, and trading volume is
adjusted to match, so this method's size dial is unaffected (checked: stored and real daily
turnover agree to within 3%). But it quietly breaks any figure that multiplies a *share count*
by that price, because the share count is not adjusted. Apple's "market value" on 30 June 2014
computes to 20 billion dollars inside the lab; the real figure was around 560 billion. Microsoft
and Exxon, which never split again, come out right. So the error is not a harmless scaling — it
is arbitrary per company, and it depends on splits that had not happened yet. The lab's
fundamental-factor method uses exactly this figure for its cheapness ranking, and that family is
the worst-scoring in the lab. I have journalled it separately; it needs fixing before any
value-based or size-based idea is trusted.

**My opinion:** the direction the idea proposed is dead, and I would not spend another trial on
it. Leaning a twenty-name book toward its biggest, busiest names is not a tilt toward the
benchmark — it is a concentration bet on the most crowded trade in the book, it steered straight
into the dot-com crash, and capping it made things worse rather than better. I would close the
"weight the book like the index" line entirely. What I *would* keep is the accidental finding
pointing the other way: systematically underweighting whatever is most heavily traded improved
every number at once, including a slightly smaller worst fall, and it is the cheapest, least
exotic change in this whole set. It is not enough on its own — three tenths of a point a year does
not rescue a book that keeps failing by half a point of drawdown — so I would not run it alone. I
would fold the de-crowding weights into the own-volatility brake that is already queued as the
next idea for this family, because that brake attacks the drawdown directly and this attacks it
slightly and for free, and the half point of fall that stands between this book and a real test
look is small enough that two small fixes might genuinely close it. And I would fix the broken
market-value figure before anyone writes another method that reads it.
methods.verdict: Leaning the book toward its biggest, busiest names is not a tilt but a concentration bet — up to 61% in one stock, straight into the dot-com crash. Leaning the other way, away from the crowd, quietly beat the control on everything.

methods.name: Step back to the market when the book has trailed it for a year: a relative-shortfall brake
methods.sourceRef: insight 58's second recommendation; M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT plus a relative-drawdown switch to SPY
methods.hypothesis: Every brake in the lab reads absolute risk: own volatility (M0001, M0011, M0022), the market's trend (F4's SPY-200 gate), the basket's own drawdown (M0013), a fast crash gate (M0012). None reads how the book is doing against the thing it is judged by. The four failed test looks did not fail in a crash; they failed by trailing a deposit-matched SPY steadily across 2016-2026, and no absolute brake can see that, because nothing about the book's own path looked alarming while it happened. This keeps M0032's ranking and execution verbatim -- top-20 raw cumulative residual momentum, F4's screen, the SPY-200 trend gate, monthly, equal weights, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, funded 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th of each month -- and adds exactly one switch: at each monthly rebalance, compare the book's own trailing 12-month return with SPY's over the same sessions, and while the book is behind by more than the threshold, park a fraction of the account in SPY. I expect this to COST return on the dev window, and the point of the run is to price the insurance rather than hope it is free. The useful outputs are two numbers the lab has never measured: how many points a year the switch costs, and how often and how long it fires. A brake that costs under a point a year and caps the relative shortfall is a far better promotion candidate than one more ranking tweak, because the failure it insures against is the one that has now actually happened four times out of four. CTRL (park = 0) is the in-method control: it should reproduce M0032's trade count and shape on the identical window and fee schedule, which is the only fair baseline, since a recorded trial's returns are not reproducible across store rebuilds and must be compared re-run to re-run.
methods.expectedFailure: The switch sells low and buys the index back high, at least twice. 1996-2015 contains two long spells -- 1998-2000 and 2007-2009 -- in which an active book trailing the index was exactly the moment to keep holding the active book: momentum lags badly into the late stage of a melt-up and then earns it all back in the unwind. Being wrong twice in twenty years can easily cost more than the two points a year the switch is trying to protect, so I expect the braked variants to land 1-3 points a year below CTRL with a worst fall that is no better, and possibly worse, because the parked SPY leg takes the market's own 2008 fall at full size while the trend gate that would have held the stock book in cash is still shut. The second way it fails is quieter and worse: the trigger almost never fires on dev, because a top-20 residual-momentum book beat SPY by seven points a year over 1996-2015, so a 12-month shortfall of 10 or 15 points is rare -- and then the dev window says nothing at all about the regime that actually broke the four test looks, and every variant comes back as a near-copy of CTRL.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

**What this is.** Every safety switch in the lab so far watches the book itself: how jumpy it has
been, how far it has fallen from its own high, whether the market is above its one-year average.
None of them watches the one thing the method is actually judged on — whether it is keeping up
with simply buying the market. That matters, because all four of the lab's spent test-window looks
failed the same way. Not one of them blew up. They just quietly trailed the market, for years,
while nothing about their own behaviour looked wrong.

So this run asked a simple question. Take the best real-fee book in the lab — rank stocks on how
much they moved after taking out the part the whole market explains, hold the best twenty in
fractional shares, stand aside when the market is below its 200-day average, 5 million rupiah in
on the 25th of every month, Gotrade's real fees — change nothing about it, and bolt on one switch:
**when the book has been behind the market over the last twelve months by more than X, move some
of the account into the market itself until it catches up.** Six versions were registered before
any result: a control with the switch off, then "behind by more than 5, 10 or 15 points" at half
the account, and 10 or 15 points at the whole account.

**The answer: the insurance costs between a tenth of a point and a point and a sixth a year, and
on this window it buys nothing at all.**

| version | switch fires when | moves | your money earned | worst fall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CTRL (switch off) | — | — | **+13.7% a year** | 20.6% |
| behind >15 points | rarely | half | +13.6% | 20.6% |
| behind >15 points | rarely | all of it | +13.4% | 20.6% |
| behind >10 points | sometimes | half | +13.1% | 20.6% |
| behind >5 points | often | half | +13.0% | 20.6% |
| behind >10 points | sometimes | all of it | **+12.5%** | 20.6% |

The same deposits put into the market instead earned +7.2% a year, so every version still beat the
market comfortably. Gains outweighed losses by about two to one throughout (2.0 for the control,
1.88 to 1.97 for the braked versions). The worst year was 2015, −4.1%, for all six.

**The control did its job.** With the switch off this is the parent method, M0032, re-run: same
money-weighted return to four decimal places (13.684%), same worst fall to five (20.6495%), same
1,607 trades, same profit factor. That matters more than it sounds, because a recorded old trial's
numbers are not reproducible across store rebuilds — so the braked versions are compared against a
control run in the same batch, on the same store, at the same fees, not against a number on file.

**The worst fall did not move. At all.** Every version records 20.65%, and the versions differ
only in the seventh decimal place. That is not a rounding story; it is the whole finding, and the
reason is worth stating precisely.

The book's worst fall ran from **9 May 2006 to 21 July 2006**, a drop of about 20.7%. Over the
twelve months leading into that peak the book was **ahead** of the market by 11.8 points, and a
month later still ahead by 6.0 points. The switch was off, and correctly off by its own rule. It
turned on at the end of July 2006 — **ten days after the bottom.**

That is not bad luck. It is the mechanism, and it is structural. A momentum book's worst falls
arrive immediately after its best runs: the thing that makes it fall is that the names it just
bought were the ones that had already gone furthest. A switch that waits for twelve months of
under-performance before acting is therefore *guaranteed* to be switched off at the top and
switched on near the bottom. It is a rear-view mirror pointed at the wrong road.

**It made the thing it was built to prevent worse.** This is the part that settles it. The whole
point of the switch was to stop the account falling a long way behind the market. Measured
directly — the worst the account ever did over any twelve months compared with simply buying the
market over those same twelve months:

| version | worst 12-month shortfall | share of months more than 10 points behind |
|---|---|---|
| CTRL (switch off) | **−43.6%** | **16.4%** |
| behind >15 points, half | −45.4% | 16.9% |
| behind >15 points, all of it | −47.2% | 17.3% |
| behind >5 points, half | −47.5% | 17.9% |
| behind >10 points, half | −47.5% | 18.1% |
| behind >10 points, all of it | −51.5% | 21.2% |

Every single version is **worse** than doing nothing, on the exact measure it was designed to
improve, and the version that acts hardest is worst of all. That is not a disappointing result, it
is a contradictory one, and it has a plain explanation: stepping into the market at the moment you
are furthest behind locks the shortfall in and hands away the catch-up. The gap closes when the
picker recovers — and the switch has just sold the picker.

**When it did fire, and what it cost.** At the 5-point setting the switch was on for 45 of 238
months (19% of the time), in five spells:

- June 1996 – March 1997 (10 months)
- December 1997 – June 1999 (**19 months**)
- July 2006 – June 2007 (12 months)
- January – March 2010 (3 months)
- June 2011 (1 month)

The 19-month spell is the expensive one, and it is exactly the one written down in advance as the
expected failure: through 1998 and into 1999 this kind of book lagged badly while a handful of
very large names ran away with the index — and then earned all of it back and more in 1999 and
2000. Stepping aside into the index for those nineteen months meant selling the book at its most
behind and buying it back after the catch-up had happened.

There is a sharper version of this. The **tighter** 5-point trigger fires 2.6 times as often as the
10-point one, yet costs barely more a year (0.64 points against 0.56). Per month switched on, the
deeper trigger is more than twice as expensive. Waiting for a bigger shortfall does not make the
signal better — it makes it a more precise instrument for selling the bottom, because a bigger
shortfall is simply a later point in the same unwind.

**Luck.** The lab has now tried 33 distinct methods, and every result is discounted for that: with
33 tries, some result was going to look good by chance. The measure of how likely a result is real
rather than luck (DSR) is 0.946 for the control and 0.911 to 0.943 for the braked versions, against
a bar of 0.90. All six clear it. That is not a reprieve: clearing the luck bar only means the
return is probably real, and the return here is *worse* than the control's. Adding the switch
lowered the luck score as well as the return, which is what you would expect from a change that
adds trades without adding edge.

**Did it fail its go-live conditions?** Yes — all six fail the same single condition the parent
failed, a worst fall of 20.6% against a 20% limit, and they fail it by the same amount. The switch
was aimed squarely at that condition and moved it by less than a hundredth of a point.

**Hypothesis and expected failure.** The hypothesis was that this would cost return and that the
price was worth measuring. That held: it cost 0.13 to 1.17 points a year. The expected failure was
written in two parts. The first — "it sells low and buys back high, at least twice, in 1998-2000
and 2007-2009" — happened, and the 1998-99 spell is where most of the cost came from. The second —
"the trigger almost never fires, so every version comes back as a near-copy of the control" —
did **not** happen, and that is the one genuinely useful thing here: the trigger fires often
enough (19%, 7% and 2% of months at the three settings) that the result is a real measurement of
the idea and not a null run. The idea got a fair hearing and lost.

**Comparison with the parent.** M0032 ran at the same fees on the same preset and recorded +13.7%
money-weighted against the market's +7.2%, a 20.6% worst fall, profit factor 1.98 and 1,607 trades.
The control here reproduces that exactly, so every number above is a like-for-like comparison, real
fees against real fees, fractional shares against fractional shares.

**What I could not do honestly, and what I assumed.** The allocator never sees the account's
balance, so "how has the book done over the last twelve months" had to be rebuilt from prices: at
each month-end inside the window the unbraked ranking is recomputed and those equal-weight baskets
are chained day by day. Three assumptions, all written into the method file before the run:

1. The trigger tracks the **unbraked** book, not the real account, so that parking in the market
   cannot mechanically close its own gap and switch itself off.
2. It uses the current month's index membership when recomputing past months, because
   point-in-time membership can only reach an allocator through a path the lab reserves for
   company-filing data (this store's filing coverage is 32%, under the 80% floor). Measured on this
   store, that approximation overlaps the true historical membership by 94-98% a year back — about
   12 extra names out of 250-390. It affects only the trigger's universe, never the book's own
   picks, which use the true historical membership.
3. The trigger reads about 677 days of history where the method declares 401. The declared figure
   is what the *picks* need, kept deliberately equal to the parent's so both run over an identical
   window and stay comparable trade for trade. Where the deeper history is absent the switch simply
   stays off.

The shared test fixture is only 473 days long, so the standard contract test cannot reach the
switch at all. It was therefore checked directly against the real market before the run: the
trigger is measurable from the very first day of the window with no gaps, it reproduces identically
whether run on full history or on history cut off at the decision date, it never reads a future
bar, the weights always sum to at most one, and when the market's own trend filter is shut the
switch correctly adds nothing — which is visible on 30 September 1998, where the trigger was firing
and the book correctly stayed in cash rather than buying the index.

**What the three runs of this batch say together.** Two sibling methods ran the same week against
the same wall, and read side by side they localise the problem precisely.

- Changing **which names you pick** does not move the worst fall. The frog-in-the-pan picker tried
  five different ways of choosing and landed between 22.2% and 22.8%, a span of six tenths of a
  point across completely different books.
- Changing **when you hold less** does not move it either. That is this method: six versions, every
  one at 20.6%, identical to four decimal places.
- Changing **how much you hold, all the time**, does move it. The own-volatility sibling, run on
  this same book at these same fees, reached a 16.4% worst fall at its hardest setting and cleared
  every go-live condition — but it got there by holding less in every market, good and bad, and it
  gave up about two points of yearly return to do it. Its gentler settings, which de-risk only
  sometimes, stayed stuck at 19.9-20.0% like everything else.

So the honest shape of the lab's drawdown problem is this: **the worst fall only moves when you
hold less all the time, not when you hold less sometimes.** Every conditional switch tried so far —
a market trend filter, a basket drawdown brake, a crash gate, a gentle volatility target, and now a
relative-shortfall switch — is off going into a fast fall and on during the recovery, because all
of them need the fall to have started before they can see it. The falls that bind here are
six-week, market-wide events, and six weeks is not enough time for a monthly signal to help. That
is a reaction-speed limit, and no amount of threshold tuning gets around it.

**My opinion:** this direction is dead in this shape, I would not spend another trial on a
threshold or a step size, and I would not spend a test-window look on any version of it. The idea
behind it is still right — four of four failed looks failed by trailing the market, and nothing in
the lab watches for that — but this run shows that *trailing over the last twelve months* is the
wrong thing to watch, and shows why in a way no further setting will change. The signal is backward
looking by a full year while the damage is front-loaded: by the time the book is twelve months
behind, the under-performance has already been paid for, and what is left to sell is the catch-up.
Three thresholds and two step sizes all cost return, all left the worst fall untouched to four
decimal places, and all made the relative shortfall worse. That last one is the clincher — a
treatment that reliably worsens the symptom it targets is not under-tuned, it is pointed the wrong
way.

Two things follow, and I have queued the first.

**The mirror is the promising question.** The measurement that killed this method is also the most
useful thing it produced: the book's worst fall began when it was eleven and a half points *ahead*
of the market over the previous year. That is a condition you can see at the time, not a year late,
and it is aimed at the one go-live condition this entire family still fails — a 20.6% worst fall
against a 20% limit, missed by about six tenths of a point and nothing else. So the next method
keeps M0032 and M0035's machinery verbatim and only inverts the comparison: trim the stock book
toward the market when it is a long way **ahead**, not when it is behind. I have registered that as
the next idea. Its own most likely failure is worth saying now — for a book that beat the market by
seven points a year on this history, "a long way ahead" may be the normal state, in which case the
method quietly becomes a permanent part-market core wearing a disguise, and the honest version of
it is the one the lab already has.

**And on the original problem, a caution against the obvious next move.** The tempting reading of
the four failed looks is "watch how narrow the market is and step aside when breadth collapses".
The lab has already measured that and the answer is discouraging: labelling months by whether the
index beat the average member does not separate the recent era from the old one, and what does
separate them — three years of that gap running persistently one way — happened on this history
exactly once, in six of two hundred and two windows. The old window simply does not contain the
regime that broke the four looks, at strength. So I would not trust any switch tuned to spot it
here, including a well-intentioned breadth gate. The protection that does show up on this history
is the dull structural one, holding part of the account in the market permanently rather than
conditionally; the lab's core-plus-satellite method does that and is dev-eligible, though it was
measured at the old flat fee of a tenth of a percent a trade, so its numbers are not directly
comparable with the real-fee ones above and it would need a real-fee twin before anyone promoted
it.
methods.verdict: Stepping back to the market after a year of trailing it cost 0.1 to 1.2 points a year, left the worst fall unmoved at 20.6%, and made the shortfall it was built to cap WORSE on every setting: the book's worst fall began while it was 11.8 points ahead of the market, so the switch was off throughout and turned on ten days after the bottom.

methods.name: Frog in the pan: prefer momentum earned in a drizzle over momentum earned in jumps
methods.sourceRef: Da, Gurun & Warachka (2014), Frog in the Pan: Continuous Information and Momentum, Review of Financial Studies 27(7), 2171-2218 (SSRN 1777988)
methods.hypothesis: Da, Gurun and Warachka's frog-in-the-pan result says investors under-react to information that arrives as a long drizzle of small daily moves and over-react to the same cumulative move delivered in a few jumps, so momentum earned smoothly continues while momentum earned in jumps reverses. The measure needs nothing the store lacks: information discreteness is sign(formation return) times (share of down days minus share of up days) over the formation window, computed from daily returns alone. In the paper, six-month momentum profits fall monotonically from 8.86% a year for the most continuous information to 2.91% for the most discrete at the same cumulative formation return, and the finding carries a replicated status. The lab has now ranked on the LEVEL of past return eleven different ways and has never once asked HOW that return was earned, which makes this the cheapest genuinely new signal available on the data already on disk. This method keeps M0032's frame -- F4's liquidity and membership screen, the SPY-200 trend gate, top-20, monthly, equal weights, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, funded 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th of each month -- and changes only how the twenty names are chosen out of the winners. CONT takes the forty highest 12-1 momentum names and holds the twenty most continuous of them; DISC is the paper's mirror and holds the twenty most discrete, which the hypothesis says must be the worst of the set and is the control that makes the others mean anything; BLEND ranks the whole eligible set on momentum rank plus continuity rank together. RM-CONT and RM-DISC are the same pair with the pool drawn on M0007-N20-RAW's raw residual momentum instead of total momentum, which is the lab's best dev ranking key, so the two engines are tested for whether continuity adds anything on top of the best thing already known. I expect continuity to show up first in the gains-to-losses ratio and the worst fall rather than in the return, because its mechanism is fewer reversals among the picks. A smaller worst fall at the same return is the result that would matter most here, since the worst fall is the only go-live condition the real-fee residual book fails.
methods.expectedFailure: Halving the candidate pool before taking twenty names forces the book down into stocks ranked 20-40 on momentum, and the momentum given up is worth more than the continuity bought: CONT lands below the plain book on return without buying back enough of the worst fall to pay for it. The second way it fails is that the mirror does not separate: DISC comes in at or above CONT, which would say the lab's universe -- 539 large, liquid, index-member names with a 20M USD dollar-volume floor -- has had the attention-limited under-reaction arbitraged out of it, since the paper's effect is strongest in small, thinly covered stocks and this universe holds none of them. The third is simple redundancy on the residual side: continuity is partly a volatility measure in disguise (a name that moves in a drizzle has a low daily spread), so RM-CONT may just re-derive the low-volatility tilt M0021 already bought, adding a trial and no information.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

**The question.** Every method this lab has tried so far ranks stocks on **how much** they went up
in the past year. Eleven different ways of measuring that, and not one of them ever asked **how**
the stock got there. A stock that drifted up two cents a day for a year and a stock that sat still
for eleven months and then jumped 40% on one announcement look identical to all of them.

A 2014 paper by Da, Gurun and Warachka says those two stocks behave very differently afterwards.
Their argument is about attention. A long drizzle of tiny daily moves is easy to ignore — nobody
reacts to a 0.2% day — so the news gets priced in slowly and the stock keeps drifting up after you
buy it. One big jump is impossible to ignore, everybody piles in at once, the price overshoots, and
it gives some of it back. They call it the frog in the pan: the frog notices the pot being thrown
into the fire, not the water warming one degree at a time.

The measure costs nothing. For each stock, over the past year, count the up days and the down days.
A stock that rose on 55% of days and fell on 45% earned its year in a drizzle. A stock with the same
total gain that rose on only 48% of days must have got there on a handful of enormous days. That is
the whole signal, and daily prices are all it needs.

**What I ran.** The same machinery as your current best book — the big liquid index names, equal
money in twenty of them, rebalanced monthly, standing aside entirely whenever the market itself is
below its 200-day average, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, and your real funding of
10,000,000 rupiah to open plus 5,000,000 rupiah on the 25th of every month — 237 deposits, 149,338
dollars of your own money in all. Nothing about the trading changed. Only the choice of which twenty
names to hold.

Five versions, all written down before anything was run:

* **the drizzle book** — take the forty highest one-year gainers, then keep the twenty that earned
  it most smoothly;
* **the jumps book** — the exact mirror: the same forty, keep the twenty that earned it most
  abruptly. This one exists to be the control. If the idea is real, this must be the worst of the
  set; if it is not worse, there is nothing here;
* **the combined book** — no pool at all, score every name on gain and smoothness together;
* **the same two again**, but drawing the forty from your current best ranking (the residual one,
  which strips out the part of a stock's move that was just the whole market moving) instead of
  from the plain one-year gain.

**The results**, on 1996 to October 2015, all at real fees on your real deposits:

| | your money earned | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades | how much it churned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the drizzle book | **+12.1% a year** | 22.8% | 2.09 | 1,203 | 6.4x |
| the combined book | +12.0% | 22.3% | **2.17** | 1,199 | 6.4x |
| the jumps book (control) | **+9.8%** | 22.7% | 1.72 | 1,582 | 8.4x |
| drizzle, on the residual ranking | +11.9% | 22.2% | 1.85 | 1,714 | 9.3x |
| jumps, on the residual ranking | +12.0% | 22.6% | 1.83 | 1,751 | 9.5x |
| *the same deposits put into SPY* | *+7.2%* | — | — | — | — |
| *your current best book, for scale* | *+13.7%* | *20.6%* | *1.98* | *1,607* | *8.9x* |

**In money.** On the same 149,338 dollars paid in, the drizzle book ended at **572,347 dollars** and
its mirror at **435,500 dollars** — a 137,000-dollar difference, 31% more money, from nothing but
asking how the gains were earned. The combined book ended at 563,742, the two residual versions at
559,894 and 566,548 (again, indistinguishable from each other), and the book you already have at
694,730. All six of those balances come from one single re-run of all six on the same day, so they
are comparable with each other even though a recorded trial's own stored total is not reproducible
against a fresh run.

"Your money earned" is the money-weighted return — the rate your actual deposits actually grew at,
with the market line fed the identical dollars on the identical days, so neither side gets credit
for lucky timing. "Gains vs losses" is total money made on winning trades divided by total money
lost on losing ones. "How much it churned" is how many times over the book replaced itself.

**The headline: the effect is real, and it is big.** The drizzle book earned 12.1% a year. Its
mirror, built from the same forty candidates on the same days with the same fees, earned 9.8%. That
is 2.3 percentage points a year, every year, for twenty years, bought purely by asking how the gain
was earned rather than how large it was. The gap shows up on every other measure too: gains against
losses 2.09 versus 1.72, and the drizzle book replaced its holdings 24% less often. It is not a
rounding error and it is not one lucky year.

**Why it works.** Smooth winners stay winners. That is visible directly in the churn: the drizzle
book made 1,203 trades where the jumps book made 1,582 — a quarter fewer. Each of those extra
trades is a name that was bought because it had just spiked, then faded out of the top twenty and
had to be sold. Those are the losing trades, and taking fewer of them is exactly what lifts the
gains-to-losses ratio from 1.72 to 2.09. As a bonus, it also pays less in fees, because it trades
less.

**And the headline on the other side: it bought nothing at all on the fall.** Every one of the five
lost between 22.2% and 22.8% from a peak, and the limit is 20%. So the method is rejected. Worse,
all five fell further than the book they were built on, which lost 20.6%. Whichever way the twenty
names were chosen, the fall was the same.

That is not a mystery once you look at when the falls happened. The drizzle book's worst fall ran
from 7 July to 22 August 2011 — six weeks, the debt-ceiling fight and the euro scare. The combined
book's and the residual drizzle book's worst falls both ran from 17 July to 31 August 1998 — six
weeks, Russia defaulting and the LTCM hedge fund blowing up. These are market-wide crashes that
arrive in weeks. The 200-day average that this book uses to step aside takes months to turn, so it
was still fully invested when they hit, and when the whole market drops 15% in six weeks it does
not matter one bit whether your twenty names got their gains smoothly or in jumps. **Choosing better
names cannot fix a fall caused by owning stocks at all.** Only owning less — a brake on position
size — can.

**The mirror died on the residual ranking, and that is the most useful thing here.** On the plain
one-year ranking, drizzle beat jumps by 2.3 points. On the residual ranking, drizzle earned 11.90%
and jumps earned 11.99% — identical, and if anything the wrong way round. Gains-to-losses 1.85
against 1.83. Nothing. The signal that was worth 2.3 points a year on one pool was worth zero on
the other.

My first guess was that the residual ranking already prefers smooth names, leaving nothing to sort.
I measured it rather than assuming it, on 76 quarterly dates across the window, and **that guess was
wrong.** Average smoothness of the forty names picked by plain gain: +0.065. Of the forty picked by
the residual ranking: +0.052 — *less* smooth, not more. And the spread of smoothness inside the
residual pool was slightly *wider* (0.053 against 0.049), so there was, if anything, more to sort
on, not less. The two pools only share about 18 of their 40 names, so they really are different
books.

What I think is actually going on: **I measured the wrong return stream.** The residual ranking
scores a stock on its move after the market's own move is taken out. But I counted up days and down
days on the stock's *total* daily return — market move included. For a stock chosen because its
market-adjusted drift was steady, the up-and-down pattern of its raw price is mostly the market's
pattern, not the stock's, so the count says nothing about the thing the ranking cared about. The
matched pair separated by 2.3 points; the mismatched pair separated by zero. That is a clean reading
and it points directly at the next experiment: count the up and down days of the *residual* returns,
the same stream the residual ranking is built on. I have queued it.

The honest alternative is duller: the effect simply is not there for residual winners. I cannot rule
it out from this run. But the measurement above rules out the "nothing left to sort" story, and
"measure the path of the same thing you ranked on" is a cheap and specific test that settles it
either way.

**How likely is this to be real rather than luck?** The lab scores that with a number called DSR,
which discounts a result by how many different ideas have been tried — because if you try enough
things, something will look good by accident. The lab counts 31 distinct methods now, and your bar
since 7 October is 0.90. The drizzle book scores 0.923, the combined book 0.924, both residual
versions 0.937 and 0.943. All clear the bar. The jumps book scores 0.799 and does not — which is
itself the right answer, since it is the version that is supposed to be bad. Note the irony worth
keeping in mind: the *highest* luck score in this batch, 0.943, belongs to the jumps-on-residual
book, a configuration I registered in advance as meaningless. That score measures steadiness, not
whether an idea makes sense.

**Worst year, and how much of the time it was invested.** The drizzle book's worst calendar year was
2011, down 4.2%. The combined book's was 2006, down just 1.0%. All five were invested about 69.5% of
the time — identical to the book they came from, which is expected, since the market trend gate was
untouched.

**Did the hypothesis hold?** Half of it, and I said in advance which half I expected. I wrote that
smoothness would show up "first in the gains-to-losses ratio and the worst fall rather than in the
return." It showed up strongly in gains-to-losses (2.09 against 1.72) and in the return (2.3 points
a year, more than I expected). It showed up in the worst fall **not at all** — and I had written that
"a smaller worst fall at the same return is the result that would matter most here." That is the
result I wanted and did not get.

**Did the expected failure happen?** Partly, and in a way that is worth recording precisely.

* I feared the mirror would fail to separate — that this universe of 539 big, heavily watched names
  would have had the effect arbitraged out of it, since the paper's effect is strongest in small,
  ignored stocks. **That did not happen on the plain ranking.** It is alive and worth 2.3 points a
  year even among the most watched companies in America. That genuinely surprised me.
* I feared halving the pool would cost more momentum than the smoothness was worth. **Not against
  the control it was registered against** — the drizzle book beat the jumps book clearly. But I have
  to be straight about a gap: the lab has never run the plain twenty-name one-year-gain book at real
  fees on your real deposits, so I cannot tell you whether the drizzle book beats *that*. The only
  clean comparison this run supports is drizzle against jumps, and that one it wins.
* I feared the residual side would be redundant. **It was worse than redundant — it was empty**, and
  measuring it told me why I had probably built it wrong.

**Compared with your current best book.** All five of these lose to it: 12.1% at a 22.8% fall against
13.7% at a 20.6% fall. Both were measured the same way, at the same real fees, on the same deposits,
in the same run, so that comparison is apples to apples with nothing hidden. The smoothness idea, as
built here, does not improve on what you already have.

**My opinion:** this direction is worth more trials, but not the ones I just ran. The finding that
