- **The jump was the edge, not the volume.** The earnings-day book, built on heavy volume *with* an up jump, earned +11.6% a year against SPY's +7.2% in its monthly form. Take the jump away and the edge is gone. Removing the move cap (ANYMOVE) did not help either, because with a symmetric cap removed the book catches down-jumps as well as up-jumps. The direction of the news matters, and volume alone does not say which way it went.
- **Turnover at real fees.** The book replaces almost every name every month (2,400 trades over twenty years). At Gotrade's fee on a 5% slot of a small account, that is several tenths of a point a year handed over. On an edge this thin, that decides the result.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis did not hold: high volume did not beat low volume, and the main variant did not beat SPY in a way that counts. The expected failure happened almost word for word: the premium was too small in big stocks to survive monthly turnover at real fees, and a heavy week with no move is mostly mechanical trading, not new attention. The cash switch kept the main variant just under the 20% fall limit, better than I feared.

## Compared with near relatives

- **The earnings-day book (M0063), monthly form:** +11.6% a year, worst fall 25.2%. This method's best: +7.3%, worst fall 19.3%. The four-point difference is what the up jump was worth.
- **The busy-stock short-term winners (M0057):** that one also found the *quiet* control beating the busy picks (+8.2% against +6.5%). Two independent tests now say the same thing: among big index stocks, heavy trading on its own predicts nothing good, and slightly bad.

My opinion: this direction is finished. Volume on its own is not an edge in big US stocks after fees. Two methods now show quiet stocks beating busy ones, and the one-day window the paper used was the worst variant here. What *did* work is volume as a sign that news arrived, combined with which way the price went. That is the earnings-day book, and its open problem is its 1998 fall, not its signal. I would not spend another id on volume-visibility. I would spend it on that book: a version that only takes a jump when it lands well above a stock's normal daily range, so routine big days are left out.
methods.verdict: Rejected: heavy trading without a price move tied SPY (+7.3% vs +7.2% a year) and failed the luck test; the quietest stocks did better than the busiest, so volume alone is not the edge

methods.name: Earnings-day jumps measured against the stock's own normal swing: only take a news day that is large for that stock
methods.hypothesis: The monthly earnings-day book beat SPY by 4.4 points a year but fell 25% in 1998, and M0071 showed volume alone carries no edge, so the jump is the signal. A fixed 4-point jump threshold treats a calm utility and a volatile chip stock alike; dividing the three-day market-adjusted jump by the stock's own 60-day daily volatility (a standardised surprise, as in standardised unexpected earnings) should keep the genuinely surprising news days and drop routine big days of jumpy stocks, which are the names that fell hardest in summer 1998. Same frame as M0063-M-N20-TREND (volume at least 3x median, up gap, monthly, 20 slots, rest SPY, SPY-200 switch, fractional at real fees); variants: standardised jump at least 2 and at least 3 sigma, ranked by sigma, plus the raw-jump control. Success: worst fall under 20% with the excess over SPY kept, and positive in 2009-2015. Expected failure: the 1998 fall was market-wide and the switch was late, so better picks may not shrink it.

methods.name: Turnaround losers: big companies that fell hardest over five years but have risen over the past year
methods.hypothesis: M0069 showed that buying five-year losers pays only through crashes and rebounds, and that most of its fall comes from buying companies still falling (2001-2002, 2008). Require the second half of a turnaround before buying: among index members in the bottom fifth by the months -60..-13 return, hold the 20 with the best last-12-month return (or simply a positive one, and price above the 200-day average), equal weight, fractional at Gotrade's real fees, empty slots in SPY. This should keep the 2000-2002 old-economy rotation and the 2009-2010 recovery while skipping falling knives. Expected failure: the filter turns it into a momentum book among cheap names, so its month-to-month result may move with the failed momentum books (the gate's behaviour kin) and the 2009 bounce, which came off a bottom with negative trailing returns, is lost; also survivorship still flatters the losers that lived.

methods.name: Big dividend raisers as a tilt inside a market-shaped book: the 100 most-traded members, half the money in SPY
methods.hypothesis: M0070 showed a 25%+ dividend raise beats steady payers by about 2 points a year in every era, but an equal-slot payer book loses to SPY's big-company drift after 2009 (-3.1 points a year for the big-raise book). Keep the signal and remove the size bet: only members in the top 100 by 60-day dollar volume, raises of 25%+ or first payments held six months, up to 10 names at 5% each, with at least 50% always in SPY, re-picked monthly at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares. Variants: with and without the SPY-200 cash switch, and the 50%-SPY core with steady payers as the control. Success means beating SPY in 2009-2015 with a worst fall under 20%. Expected failure: with half in SPY and 10 slots, the excess shrinks to about one point a year, too little to pass the luck check, and the 2011 fall still lands near the limit.

methods.name: The earnings-day book behind a fast crash exit with slow, monthly re-entry
methods.hypothesis: M0066 showed a trailing-volatility brake cannot defend the news-day book: the 1998 fall started as a calm slide in April, so a one-month volatility reading never engaged (best: 20.2% fall without deposits at a 14% target), and the brake then held cash through the 2009 rebound (+50% cut to +21%), losing to SPY in 2009-2015. M0066-W-MTREND also showed the SPY-200 switch must not be re-read weekly: reading it monthly took the weekly-pick book from +5.0% to +10.9% a year on the owner's deposits. So split the switch: exit fast, enter slow. Keep M0063-M-N20-TREND's picks (and W-MTREND's weekly picks as a second variant) and the monthly SPY-200 switch, and add M0012's fast crash gate (SPY's own sudden fall over days) checked weekly on monthly-rank-weekly-resize-frac-gotrade; once it fires, the book stays in cash until the next monthly check finds SPY above its 200-day average. Expected failure: the 1998 slide from April was slow, so a gate keyed to a sudden few-day drop may fire only in August, after most of the 23.6% fall; published 2008, so it may have faded by 2016.

methods.name: Buy the big dividend raise on the day it is announced, not weeks later when it goes ex
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0070 (R25-H6-T close miss); Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), JF 50(2); declaration dates from the one-month EODHD pull (2026-10-10)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1994-1995, so most of the dev window is after the crowd could know the dividend-change drift. M0070's big-raise book (latest dividend >= 25% over the median of the up-to-four prior payments in 400 days and at most double, or a first payment; up to 20 F4-screened members at 5% while the event is under 182 days old, held names first then the newest event, rest in SPY, monthly, behind the SPY-200 switch, fractional at Gotrade's real fees) beat SPY by 3.7 points a year on the deposits but only saw each raise on its ex-date, a median 19-20 days after the board declared it (the store now has declaration dates for 85-93% of dividends each year 1996-2015). If part of the drift happens between declaration and ex-date, acting on the declaration day should add return. Paired design, pre-registered: each announced variant (event date = declaration date, else the ex-date) has an ex-date twin with identical rules; the hold clock, baseline and ranking run on each arm's own event date. A-M / X-M monthly re-pick (X-M should reproduce M0070-R25-H6-T); A-W / X-W re-pick weekly so a monthly clock does not waste a 20-day head start (weekly-hold-frac-gotrade, no preset exists, dev only); A-M-D / X-M-D monthly counting only dividends that carry a declaration date, in both arms, so coverage gaps cannot blur the pair. The quantity of interest is announced minus ex on funded CAGR, worst fall, DSR, 2009-2015 and walk-forward folds; passing the gate is secondary. Success for the data: A-W beats X-W and A-M beats X-M by a point a year or more, with the declared-only pair agreeing in sign.
methods.expectedFailure: The announcement-day jump (a percent or two for a raise) happens in one day, before even the weekly book can buy at the next open, while the slow months-long drift M0070 caught is the same in both arms, so the paired difference is about zero. The monthly pair differs little anyway: a 20-day earlier sighting often lands in the same monthly re-pick. Exiting 20 days earlier may give back drift as easily as it gains it. The weekly arms pay more Gotrade fees on 5% slots and the weekly SPY resize, which may eat any gain. M0070's own weaknesses carry over: worst fall near the 20% limit (21.9% in 1998-2002 fast falls before the switch turns), and lagging SPY in 2009-2015 when big-company growth led. A widely published anomaly from the 1990s: even a real dev edge is likely to fade after 2015. Withholding tax on dividends is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## The question

The owner paid for a month of data that gives the **day each dividend was announced**. Until then the lab only knew the day a dividend **went ex**, which is the day a new buyer stops getting that payment. In the dev years the announcement came a median **19-20 days** before the ex-date. The new data has an announcement date for 85-93% of dividends in every year from 1996 to 2015.

The best user of dividend news so far is M0070's **big-raise book**. It buys up to 20 big index companies whose latest dividend was at least 25% above their usual payment (or was a first payment). It holds each for six months at 5% of the money, keeps the rest in SPY, re-picks once a month and steps into cash while SPY is below its 200-day average. It beat SPY on the owner's deposits (+10.9% a year vs +7.2%). But it fell 21.9% at its worst, over the 20% limit, and it saw each raise only on the ex-date.

The question was simple: **if the book sees the raise three weeks earlier, does it earn more?**

## How it was tested: pairs

Each test is a pair with identical rules. The only difference is the day the book first sees the raise:

- **A** = announcement day (or the ex-date when no announcement date exists)
- **X** = ex-date, the way M0070 did it

Three pairs were fixed before any result:

- **A-M / X-M**: re-pick monthly. X-M is exactly M0070's best version.
- **A-W / X-W**: re-pick **weekly**, so a three-week head start is not lost waiting for the month's turn. This trades on a weekly fractional real-fee setup that has no preset yet, so it can run on dev but could not be promoted.
- **A-M-D / X-M-D**: monthly, counting only dividends that *have* an announcement date, in both arms. This way the 13% with no date cannot blur the comparison.

**Sanity check:** X-M reproduced M0070's best version to the last digit: same 540 trades, +10.9% a year funded, 21.9% worst fall. So the harness is sound and the pairs are fair.

## Results (on the owner's deposits, Gotrade's real fees, 1996-2015)

| pair | announced | ex-date | difference | worst fall A / X |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| monthly | +10.3% a year | +10.9% | **−0.6 pt** | 21.3% / 21.9% |
| weekly | +5.0% | +6.1% | **−1.1 pt** | 32.0% / 32.7% |
| monthly, dated only | +10.5% | +10.8% | **−0.3 pt** | 21.2% / 21.1% |

SPY with the same deposits earned +7.2% a year.

**On the paired difference** (the value of the data), using monthly returns with the deposits taken out:

- Monthly pair: announced trailed by 0.036% a month on average. That is about 0.4 points a year. It was ahead in only 6 of 20 years. The t-statistic is −0.76, so this is statistically **indistinguishable from zero**, and the sign is negative.
- Weekly pair: −0.039% a month (t = −0.84), ahead in 9 of 20 years.
- Dated-only pair: −0.014% a month (t = −0.30), ahead in 9 of 20 years.

**All three pairs agree in sign, and the sign is the wrong one.** Seeing the raise three weeks earlier did not add return. If anything, it cost a little.

**The 2009-2015 years**, the ones most like today (no deposits, per year):

- monthly: announced +12.4% vs ex-date +13.4%
- weekly: +6.1% vs +8.7%
- dated only: +12.9% vs +13.6%

The announced arm was behind in every pair. Walk-forward (`lab walkforward`): the method won 2 of 4 folds, which is not a majority. Its pick trailed SPY by 2.7 points a year in 2009-2015. That is the same weakness M0070 had.

**Luck check (DSR at N = 50 methods, bar 0.90):** the monthly arms pass. A-M scored 0.932 and X-M 0.946, meaning a result this good is unlikely to be pure luck after 50 tries. The weekly arms fail badly (0.57-0.62). This says nothing new, though. The arms that pass are M0070 restated.

**Worst fall:** every monthly arm is between 21.1% and 21.9%, so all of them miss the 20% limit by a hair. It happens in the same fast falls M0070 hit, before the 200-day switch turns. The worst calendar year was 2011 (−6% to −9%).

## Why

1. **The jump at the announcement is too fast to catch.** When a board announces a big raise, the price reacts that day. A book that sees the news at the close and buys at the next open has already missed it. The slow drift that follows over months is what M0070 earned, and both arms catch it equally.
2. **The early arm also leaves early.** Each arm holds for six months from the day it saw the raise, so the announced arm sells about three weeks sooner. Any drift late in the window goes to the ex-date arm instead.
3. **Picking order changes a little, and that is noise.** With 20 slots and "newest event first", the earlier date sometimes swaps one stock for another. That reshuffle is what made the year-by-year differences swing between +4 and −3 points, with no pattern.

## The weekly clock costs more than the timing

Both weekly arms lost about 5 points a year against their monthly twins, and fell around 32% at worst instead of 21%. Checking the SPY 200-day switch every week makes the book jump in and out of the market far more often (927 trades against 546). The book gets caught on the wrong side of fast reversals in 2000-2002 and 2013, and pays Gotrade's fees on every 5% slot each time. A weekly clock only pays when the signal is fast. This one is slow.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis** (announced beats ex-date by a point a year or more): **rejected**. All three pairs came out between 0.3 and 1.1 points *behind*, and none of the differences is statistically meaningful.
- **Expected failure** ("the jump is gone in a day, the drift is identical in both arms, the difference is about zero"): **happened as written**, along with the extra weekly fee and whipsaw cost and the familiar 20% miss.

## My opinion

The announcement dates were worth having. They answered a real question cleanly, and the answer is no. For a monthly or weekly book of big companies, *when* you learn about a dividend raise does not matter. What matters is *that* the company raised it, and the months of drift after. I would stop spending ids on earlier timing for this book. I would use the new data in a different way: **the market's reaction on the announcement day as a filter**, for example only raises where the stock beat SPY over the two days after the announcement. That uses information the ex-date never had, and the lab's earnings-jump work suggests the direction of the reaction is where the signal lives. The raise book's real problem is still the 21-22% fall and the 2009-2015 lag, and timing does not fix either one.
methods.verdict: Rejected: buying a big dividend raise on its announcement day instead of its ex-date earned 0.3-1.1 points a year LESS in all three pairs (+10.3% vs +10.9% monthly); the slow drift is the edge, the early sighting adds nothing

methods.name: Sell or skip a stock the day its board cuts or stops the dividend: a cut alarm laid over two books we already have
methods.sourceRef: Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), Price Reactions to Dividend Initiations and Omissions, JF 50(2); https://www.nber.org/papers/w4778; Grullon, Michaely & Swaminathan (2002), JB 75(3)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1994-1995, so most of the dev window is after the crowd could know it. Batch sera-20261010-1742 asks whether the paid-for dividend declaration dates improve methods we already have. A board that cuts its dividend (the new amount at most 75% of the median of its up-to-four previous payments in the prior 400 days, at least two of them) or stops it (a regular payer, three or more payments, with nothing new known 1.5 of its usual gaps after the last ex-date, in both timings: measured from a declaration made a quarter ahead it fires falsely) is followed by months of underperformance in the papers (about -11% over a year after an omission). The overlay removes such a name from the host's universe for 182 days from the alarm: a held name is sold at the host's next monthly check and a candidate is skipped for the host's next pick. Two hosts that hold the names a cut is most likely to hit, both monthly, fractional, at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade: EDJ = M0063-M-N20-TREND (news-day jumps; close miss, +4.4 points a year over SPY with a 25% worst fall) and REV = M0028-CALM-RESID (last month's calm fallers, the most cut-prone names by construction). For each host: HOST (overlay off; must reproduce the host's recorded trial), ANN (alarm on the declaration day, the ex-date where the store has no declaration date, about 13% of payments) and EX (the paired control: the identical alarm on the ex-date, which is all the store knew before the EODHD pull). The value of the data is ANN minus EX on funded CAGR, worst fall, DSR, the 2009-2015 era and the walk-forward folds; the value of the alarm itself is EX minus HOST. Assumed, not tested: the dated-only second pair is dropped because 87% of 1996-2015 payments carry a declaration date, so coverage gaps cannot move the pair much, and the six-variant cap is better spent on a second host. Success for the data: ANN beats EX on both hosts in the same direction; success for the alarm: ANN and EX both beat HOST.
methods.expectedFailure: Cuts among big index members are rare (about 30 a year in the whole store, 290 in 2008-2009), and both hosts sit in cash behind the SPY 200-day switch for most of 2008-2009, so the overlay changes few trades and every paired difference may be inside noise. The news-day host holds stocks that just jumped on good news, which rarely cut, so on EDJ the overlay should do almost nothing. The declaration lands about 19 days before the ex-date and the price falls on the declaration day itself, so neither arm escapes the first drop; the announcement arm only gains the drift between declaration and ex-date, and only when the two fall in different months of the host's monthly check. An omission has no row, so a gap in the store's dividend history (a missed payment in the data, a switch from quarterly to half-yearly) reads as an omission in both arms alike. Removing a fallen payer can also remove a bounce the reversal host was paid for, so on REV the alarm may cost money. Expected: |ANN - EX| under half a point a year on both hosts.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

The batch question: **does the dividend announcement data we paid for make our existing methods better?**

A board that cuts or stops its dividend is admitting the business is worse than the price says. Old papers (Michaely, Thaler and Womack, 1995) found such stocks kept sliding for months. So I built a "cut alarm" and laid it over two books the lab already has:

- **EDJ**, the monthly news-day book (it buys big companies right after a jump on heavy trading). On its own it made 11.6% a year on your deposits vs 7.2% for SPY, but fell 25% at its worst.
- **REV**, the calm-fallers book (it buys last month's calm stocks that dropped). These are the stocks most likely to be cutting their dividend.

The alarm fires when a dividend is at least 25% below the usual payment (a **cut**), or when a regular payer misses a payment by half a cycle (an **omission**). The stock is then off-limits for six months. A holding is sold at the book's next monthly check, and a new pick skips it.

Each book ran three ways, all at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares:
- **HOST**: no alarm. Both reproduced their old recorded results to the decimal, so the setup is sound.
- **ANN**: the alarm hears about a cut on the day the board **announces** it (the new data, about 19 days earlier).
- **EX**: the same alarm, but it only hears about the cut on the **ex-dividend date** (all we knew before buying the data).

**ANN minus EX** is what the data is worth. **EX minus HOST** is what the alarm itself is worth.

## Results (your money a year, deposits included, vs SPY's 7.2%)

| | HOST | ANN | EX | ANN − EX |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| News-day book | 11.57% | 11.36% | 11.44% | **−0.08 points** |
| Calm-fallers book | 7.48% | 7.58% | 7.53% | **+0.06 points** |
| News-day worst fall | 25.2% | 25.6% | 25.6% | 0 |
| Calm-fallers worst fall | 27.2% | 27.6% | 27.9% | −0.3 (ANN better) |
| News-day, 2009-2015 edge over SPY | +1.4 | +0.4 | +0.3 | +0.1 |
| Calm-fallers, 2009-2015 edge over SPY | −7.9 | −7.9 | −7.9 | 0 |

(The 2009-2015 rows use the books without deposits, in points a year above SPY.)

Walk-forward: the method won 3 of its 4 test folds (a fold trains on earlier years and then scores later years it has not seen). The two timings are too alike for the folds to tell them apart.

**Luck check (DSR):** this measures how likely a result is real rather than luck across all the methods the lab has tried. The bar is 0.90, and these trials were judged at N=52. The news-day versions sit right on it (0.899 to 0.906). The calm-fallers versions reach about 0.84. Those numbers come from the host books, not from the alarm.

**Gate:** every variant fails on worst fall (25-28% against the 20% limit). The calm-fallers versions also fail the luck check. Rejected, as expected: passing was never the aim.

## Did the announcement timing help?

**No, not in any way we can measure.** On the news-day book the earlier timing came out 0.08 points a year *worse*. On the calm-fallers book it came out 0.06 points a year *better*. The two results point in opposite directions, and both are far smaller than the noise between neighbouring variants. The pre-registered test of success was "ANN beats EX on both books, in the same direction". It failed. The expected failure ("|ANN − EX| under half a point on both") is exactly what happened.

**The alarm itself didn't help either.** It cost the news-day book 0.1-0.2 points a year and added 0.1 to the calm-fallers book. Both are noise. It changed very few trades: 8 or 9 extra trades in 1,214 on the news-day book, and 15-21 fewer in 2,794 on the calm-fallers book.

## Why

1. **Big companies rarely cut.** The whole store has about 30 cuts and omissions a year (about 300 in 2008-09). Very few of those stocks were in either book in the month it happened.
2. **The crash years were already handled.** Both books step out to cash when SPY falls below its 200-day average. That covered most of 2008-09, when the cuts were concentrated.
3. **The earlier timing is mostly wasted on a monthly book.** The announcement comes about 19 days before the ex-date. The book only trades once a month, so in most cases both arms act at the same monthly check.
4. **The price drops on the announcement day itself.** Neither arm can sell before the news is public. The only thing left to capture is the slow drift afterwards, and among big index members after 1995 that drift is small.
5. **Omissions can't be timed by the data.** An omission is a missing payment, so it shows up at the same time in both arms. A pre-run check found that measuring silence from a declaration made a quarter ahead fired 401 false alarms, so both arms now measure it from the last ex-date.
6. **2009-2015 shows a cost, not a gain.** On the news-day book the alarm cut the 2009-2015 edge from +1.4 to +0.3-0.4 points. The banks and industrials that cut in 2009 were exactly the ones that later jumped on good earnings. Benching them for six months threw away the recovery.

## Caveats

- Near the end of the window (Sept-Oct 2015), a declaration whose ex-date falls after 2015-10-16 is not in the store. At most this touches the last one or two monthly checks.
- The store has no companies that later delisted or went bankrupt. Those are exactly the firms whose cuts came before a collapse. So the alarm is tested on survivors only, which undersells it. Still, that missing group sits outside both books' universes in the paper-trading years too.

## My opinion:

The announcement dates are worth nothing to a monthly book that reads dividend *cuts*, and the cut alarm itself is worth nothing to books built on big index members. I would not spend another trial on cut overlays. If the declaration data has value, it lies where timing *is* the signal: a book that trades on the announcement day itself, such as the dividend-raise buyer (M0076) or the hold-between-announcement-and-ex window (M0079), both in this batch. That's where the 19-day lead can matter, so the batch verdict on the data should come from those two, not from this one. One thing here is worth a look: in 2009-2015 the alarm took about a point a year off the news-day book by benching cutters that went on to recover. The mirror image, buying big members six months after a cut once the trend has turned up again, is a cleaner question than another overlay. I'm queuing it as an idea, not a priority.
methods.verdict: The dividend-cut alarm changed under 2% of trades; announcing-day timing vs ex-date timing differed by under 0.1 point a year, in opposite directions on the two books: the data did not help here

methods.name: A dividend raise on the same day as an earnings jump: is the pair stronger than either signal alone?
methods.sourceRef: M0063 (earnings-day jump detector); M0070 (dividend raise drift); Kane, Lee & Marcus (1984), Earnings and dividend announcements: is there a corroboration effect?, JF 39(4)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1984 (the corroboration effect) and 2008 (the earnings-day drift M0063 copies), so the dev window sees the pair after both were known; 2009-2015 is judged first. Boards often declare the dividend with the quarterly results. A raise (10% or more over the median of the up-to-four payments in the prior 400 days, at most double, or a first payment) declared within 3 sessions of an M0063 news jump (volume >= 3x the 60-day median, an up gap, a three-day return >= 4 points over SPY's) is good news told twice, and should drift harder than either alone. Inside F4's liquidity and membership screen, behind the SPY-200 switch (all cash while it is off), hold up to 20 such names at 5% each until the jump is 60 sessions old (held names first, then the biggest jumps), the rest in SPY, re-picked weekly, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees (M0063's assumed weekly-hold-frac-gotrade preset). BATCH RULE (sera-20261010-1742): each variant has a twin timed on the ex-date instead of the announcement, and the paired difference (announcement minus ex-date) on funded CAGR, worst fall, DSR, 2009-2015 and the walk-forward folds is the value of the announcement data. Dividends with no declaration date are known on their ex-date in both arms, so they are identical across a pair and cannot blur the difference (about 87% of 1996-2015 payments carry one). Variants: JOINT-ANN (raise known by declaration within 3 sessions either side of the jump) and JOINT-EX (the identical rule timed on the ex-date: almost no ex-date falls on an earnings day, so this book is expected to sit nearly all in SPY -- it is the literal control); WIN-ANN and WIN-EX (the realistic pair: the jump may come up to 45 sessions before the raise became known, so the ex-date twin is what one could trade without declaration dates -- see the raise on its ex-date, check for a jump in the two months before, hold until the jump is 60 sessions old; the announcement twin acts weeks earlier on the same pairs); RAISE-ANN and RAISE-EX (the raise alone, held 60 sessions from the day it became known, same frame and cadence: the 'raise alone' baseline). The 'jump alone' baseline is M0063-N20-TREND's recorded trial (identical event, screen, switch, slots, hold and cadence; not re-run). Success for the idea: JOINT-ANN or WIN-ANN beats both RAISE-ANN and M0063-N20-TREND on funded CAGR and 2009-2015; success for the data: each ANN beats its EX twin.
methods.expectedFailure: The joint events are too few among big caps (a few dozen a year at most) to fill 20 slots, so JOINT-ANN sits mostly in SPY behind the switch and its edge over SPY is too small to read or to clear the luck bar; the pair may beat SPY by a fraction of a point that the 1998 and 2011 fast falls (which land before the switch turns) swamp. The corroboration effect was measured on the announcement-day return, not on a two-month drift, and both parent signals are published anomalies that faded, so the pair may add nothing over the jump alone. JOINT-EX should be nearly SPY behind the switch, so a big JOINT-ANN minus JOINT-EX gap partly measures 'any picks vs none', which is why the WIN pair exists. For WIN, the ex-date twin buys the same names weeks later with less hold left, so most of the drift after an earnings day (front-loaded in the first weeks) may already be gone: the announcement twin should win, but by how much is the question. Weekly re-picks at Gotrade's real fees on $50-70 slots cost several tenths of a percent a side; M0063's weekly book lost to SPY on exactly that churn, so every variant may lag SPY however good the pairing is. Not modelled: US withholding tax on dividends.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

Companies often announce their dividend on the same day as their quarterly results. If that dividend is a **raise**, the market hears good news twice on one day: once in the profits, and once in the cash the board promises to pay. Kane, Lee and Marcus (1984) found the two announcements back each other up. This method asked whether a big company that does both on one day keeps rising for the next two months, more than one that only does one of them.

How it finds the two events:

- **The earnings jump** is the same detector the earnings-day book (M0063) uses. The research data has no earnings dates, so it looks for the footprint a report leaves: a day with at least 3 times normal trading volume, an opening gap up, and a three-day move at least 4 points better than SPY's.
- **The raise** is M0070's rule: a dividend at least 10% above the median of the last four payments (and at most double, so one-off special dividends are left out), or a company's first dividend.
- **The new ingredient** is the dividend **announcement dates** bought this month (EODHD). About 87% of 1996-2015 payments have one. Before this, the lab only saw a dividend on its **ex-date** (the day a new buyer no longer gets that payment), usually two to six weeks after the announcement.

The book: big index members only, up to 20 names at 5% each, the rest in SPY. It holds cash while SPY is below its 200-day average (the "trend switch"), re-picks weekly, and pays Gotrade's real fees on fractional shares. A name is held until its jump is 60 trading days old.

**Six variants, fixed before any result, as three pairs.** In each pair the two books follow identical rules. One learns about the dividend on its announcement day (ANN). The other learns about it on its ex-date (EX). The gap between them is what the announcement dates are worth.

| pair | rule |
|---|---|
| JOINT | a raise known within 3 trading days either side of a jump |
| WIN | a raise known up to 45 trading days after a jump. The EX twin is what you could trade without announcement dates: see the raise on its ex-date, check for a jump in the two months before it. |
| RAISE | the raise alone, held 60 trading days from when it became known |

The "jump alone" yardstick is the earnings-day book's own recorded result (M0063-N20-TREND). It uses the identical event, screen, switch, 20 slots, hold and weekly cadence, so it was not re-run.

## Results (dev window 1996 to October 2015, on the owner's monthly deposits, real fees)

"Your money per year" is the growth of the owner's own deposits (the money-weighted return). SPY means the same deposits put into SPY with dividends reinvested: **+7.2% a year**.

| variant | your money per year | worst fall | gains vs losses | trades | luck score (DSR) | 2009-2015 edge vs SPY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| JOINT-ANN | +3.8% | 32.2% | 1.76 | 227 | 0.451 | −12.0 pts/yr |
| JOINT-EX | +3.9% | 32.7% | 2.19 | 82 | 0.439 | −11.2 |
| WIN-ANN | +3.3% | 31.7% | 1.43 | 523 | 0.386 | −12.7 |
| WIN-EX | +2.9% | 30.3% | 1.39 | 480 | 0.328 | −13.0 |
| RAISE-ANN | +4.1% | 28.8% | 1.31 | 1515 | 0.505 | −11.5 |
| RAISE-EX | +4.2% | 32.2% | 1.34 | 1522 | 0.472 | −11.4 |
| *jump alone (M0063-N20-TREND)* | *+5.0%* | *35.4%* | *1.27* | *1930* | *0.394 (N=42)* | *−6.6* |
| *raise, ex-date, monthly, 6-month hold (M0070-R10-H6-T)* | *+8.1%* | *29.2%* | *2.33* | *699* | *0.810 (N=49)* | *−5.5* |

**Every variant failed.** All six lost to SPY by 3 to 4 points a year. All six fell more than 28% from a peak, against the 20% limit; the worst falls came in 2000 and in the 1998 and 2011 fast drops, which land before a 200-day switch can react. None comes near the luck bar. JOINT-EX also made fewer than 100 trades.

**Luck score.** The DSR (deflated Sharpe ratio) asks how likely a result is to be real skill rather than the best of many tries. At the lab's N = 51 independent tries (one per distinct method, the "methods" policy in force), the best variant scores 0.505 against the owner's bar of 0.90. That is a coin flip, and all six books lost money relative to SPY anyway.

**The 2009-2015 years, the first filter:** every variant trailed SPY by 11 to 13 points a year. SPY returned +16.7% a year. These books returned +4% to +5.5%.

## What the announcement dates were worth (the batch's question)

This is the paired difference, announcement-timed minus ex-date-timed. Each figure is the average gap in monthly returns between the twins, with deposits taken out, so it reads as points a year.

| pair | ANN minus EX, whole window | how sure (t-stat) | 2009-2015 only | your money/yr gap | worst fall gap | DSR gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| JOINT | +0.14 pts/yr | 0.44 | −0.72 | −0.1 | 0.5 pt gentler | +0.012 |
| WIN | +0.47 pts/yr | 1.40 | +0.28 | +0.4 | 1.4 pt deeper | +0.058 |
| RAISE | +0.31 pts/yr | 0.39 | −0.13 | −0.1 | 3.4 pt gentler | +0.033 |

In plain words: **knowing the announcement date helped by at most half a point a year, and we cannot tell that apart from luck.** A t-stat under 2 means the gap is the size random noise would produce. The best case, WIN at 1.40, has roughly a one-in-six chance of appearing by luck alone. In 2009-2015 the gap is negative in two of the three pairs. The announcement twins have slightly better luck scores in all three pairs, but each gap is a few hundredths on scores near 0.4-0.5 that are nowhere near 0.90.

Walk-forward check: the method as a whole beat SPY in **1 of 4** out-of-sample folds, with a −11.1 point edge in 2009-2015. The fold tool picks one variant per fold, so it cannot score each twin separately. The twins move together so closely (monthly correlation 0.99 for JOINT and WIN, 0.96 for RAISE) that per-twin folds would tell the same story.

## Why

1. **The frame lost before any stock was picked.** JOINT-EX holds almost nothing but SPY: its rule rarely fires, because an ex-date seldom falls on an earnings day. Yet it earned only +3.9% a year against SPY's +7.2%. Those 3.3 points are the cost of a **weekly** check on SPY's 200-day average. Around the average the switch flips in and out, and each flip pays Gotrade's fees and sells low to buy back higher. It lost 2 to 9% in 2010, 2011 and 2015, years SPY ended flat to up 15%. It also sat in cash all of 2001 and 2008. That helped in 2008 and cost little in 2001, but missed the 2009 rebound until the switch turned back on. M0063's weekly book showed the same cost (+5.0% weekly against +11.6% monthly). This method kept the weekly cadence because the reserved idea said so and because a news event wants a quick entry. That was a mistake in hindsight: the frame cost far more than any event could earn.
2. **The joint event is rare.** On a sample of dates JOINT-ANN held 1.6 stock names on average (at most 6), so 90% or more of the money sat in SPY behind the switch. Even if each joint event were excellent, 8% of the book cannot move the total much. Its gains-vs-losses ratio of 1.76 against the jump-alone book's 1.27 hints the paired picks were better trades, but on 227 trades that include the SPY parking it is not readable.
3. **Announcement timing barely matters for a slow signal.** Over two months the raise signal earns about the same whether the book enters on the announcement or three to six weeks later on the ex-date. Whatever the market does with a dividend raise, it mostly does on announcement day itself, before a weekly re-pick could act. What the ex-date book misses is small. The WIN pair is the one where acting earlier should help most, and it gained 0.47 points a year with a t-stat of 1.4: suggestive, not proven.

## Did the hypothesis hold?

**No.** The pair was not stronger than either alone. JOINT-ANN (+3.8%) trailed RAISE-ANN (+4.1%) and the jump alone (+5.0%). Measured against the frame's own baseline (JOINT-EX, about +3.9%), the jump adds about a point, the raise a fraction, and the pair nothing. The data question ("each ANN beats its EX twin") came out yes in direction for the gross monthly gap in all three pairs, but no in the owner's money for two of three, and not one gap is significant.

**The expected failure happened almost word for word.** Joint events were too few to fill the book, so it sat mostly in SPY. M0063's weekly churn and switch dragged every variant under SPY. The fast falls of 1998 and 2011 broke the 20% limit.

## Compared with the parents

- The jump alone (M0063-N20-TREND, same weekly frame): +5.0% a year, worst fall 35.4%. The pair did worse on money (+3.8%) with a gentler fall (32.2%), because it was mostly SPY.
- M0070's ex-date raise book (monthly, held six months): +8.1% a year. That is far better than this method's RAISE twins (+4.1/4.2%), which use the same raise rule held 60 trading days and re-picked weekly. The difference is the frame (monthly beats weekly, a longer hold beats a shorter one), not the dividend timing.

My opinion: the corroboration idea is dead in this form. It is too rare among big companies to carry a book, and the pairing showed no edge over the jump alone. Don't spend another id on it. The more useful lesson concerns the data the owner paid for: on every pair tried here, announcement dates are worth less than half a point a year, and that half point is not distinguishable from luck. A slow, months-long dividend signal gains almost nothing from acting a few weeks earlier. If the announcement data is to pay for itself, it will be in a **fast** use: buying within days of a raise and holding only a few weeks (M0076's question), or exiting on a cut the day it is announced (M0077's). Separately, this run is the clearest proof yet that the weekly SPY-200 switch costs about 3 points a year at real fees whatever the book holds. No future event book should run on it. The next try in this family should use the monthly frame that M0063 and M0070 both did better on.
methods.verdict: Rejected: a dividend raise on an earnings-jump day lost to SPY by over 3 points a year, no better than either signal alone; announcement dates added under half a point, within luck

methods.name: Hold a stock only between the day its dividend is announced and the day it goes ex
methods.sourceRef: Kalay & Loewenstein (1985), Predictable events and excess returns: the case of dividend announcements, JFE 14(3); Hartzmark & Solomon (2013), The dividend month premium, JFE 109(3)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1985 (Kalay and Loewenstein) and 2011-2013 (Hartzmark and Solomon), so the announcement-window premium was public for the whole dev window; it survives only if it is a steady demand effect (dividend-seeking buyers arriving before the payment) rather than a mispricing. Prices drift up from a regular dividend's announcement toward its ex-date. Batch theme (sera-20261010-1742): does the paid-for declaration date improve a method? Book: F4's members and liquidity screen behind the SPY 200-day switch, re-decided every session on a daily clock (daily-hold-frac-gotrade: monthly-hold-frac-gotrade's levers -- fractional, open limit, resize to target, Gotrade's real fees -- with a daily cadence, because a window is two to six weeks long), up to 20 names at 5% each, held names first then the newest announcement, the rest in SPY. Only regular dividends: within 99% to 200% of the median of the up to four payments in the prior 400 days (no cuts, first payments or specials). Variants. ANN-TOEX: buy at the open after a declared dividend's announcement, hold through the last close before the ex-date (the dividend is credited), sell at the ex-date's open -- the paper's window. ANN-H14 / EX-H14: the same 14-session hold (about the median window) started from the dividend's known day, which is the declaration when dated and the ex-date otherwise (ANN), or always the ex-date (EX, the control: the only timing the lab had before). ANN-H14-DEC / EX-H14-DEC: the same pair keeping only dividends with a declaration date in both arms, so coverage cannot blur the comparison. EX-TOEX is impossible (no window before an ex-date the book only learns on the ex-date), so ANN-TOEX's paired control is EX-H14-DEC. ANN-THRU: ANN-TOEX held one session more, through the ex-date's close, to include the ex-day itself. The value of the data is the paired difference ANN minus EX (funded CAGR, worst fall, DSR, the 2009-2015 era, the walk-forward folds), not the absolute result. Success for the data: ANN-H14-DEC beats EX-H14-DEC and ANN-TOEX beats EX-H14-DEC. Success for the method: a variant beats total-return SPY on dev within the 20% worst fall and keeps a positive edge in 2009-2015.
methods.expectedFailure: The announcement-window premium is a fraction of a percent per event (Kalay and Loewenstein report well under 1% over the window), while each event costs a 5% slot a buy and a sell at Gotrade's fees plus a matching SPY trim and add, about 0.5-1% of the slot each round trip at $50-70 slots; the book may trade 300-500 events a year and pay more in fees than the window earns, trailing SPY as M0051 did. The names are dividend payers, value-ish, lower-growth stocks that trailed SPY's big-company growth in 1997-2000 and from 2009, so the book may lag SPY in 2009-2015 even if the timing helps. Most of the price reaction to the announcement itself happens on the announcement day, before a next-open buy, so the announcement arm may only catch the slower run-up and ANN minus EX may be near zero. Behind the SPY-200 switch the 1998 and 2011 fast falls land before the switch turns, but at 20 x 5% plus SPY the book is close to SPY's own fall, so the worst fall should sit near the 20% limit. Not modelled and against the method: the book is credited every dividend in full, but the owner loses 15-30% of it to US withholding tax, and ANN-TOEX and ANN-THRU exist to collect dividends, so their real result is worse by roughly 0.1-0.3 points a year than the lab's.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

When a company's board **declares** a dividend, it names a future **ex-date**: the first day a buyer no longer gets that payment. Kalay and Loewenstein (1985) found prices tend to drift up from the announcement toward the ex-date, as buyers who want the dividend arrive. Until this week the lab only saw a dividend on its ex-date. The new data adds the declaration date for about 85-90% of dividends from 1996 on. This method asks the batch's question directly: **does knowing the announcement date make a better book?**

The book: big index members that pass the usual price and trading screen. It holds up to 20 of them at 5% each while they are inside a dividend window, puts the rest in SPY, and steps into cash when SPY is below its 200-day average. It is re-decided **every trading day**, because a window lasts only two to six weeks (median 20 calendar days, about 14 trading days). Only regular dividends count: no cuts, first payments or one-off specials. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, on the owner's 5,000,000 IDR monthly deposits.

Six variants, fixed before any result:

- **ANN-TOEX**: buy the day after a dividend is declared, sell on the morning of the ex-date (so the dividend is collected). This is the paper's own window.
- **ANN-THRU**: the same, held one more day through the ex-date.
- **ANN-H14 / EX-H14**: the paired test. Both hold 14 trading days. ANN starts the clock at the declaration (or the ex-date when no declaration is on file). EX always starts at the ex-date, which is all the lab could do before. **The difference between them is what the new data is worth.**
- **ANN-H14-DEC / EX-H14-DEC**: the same pair, keeping only dividends that have a declaration date in both arms, so gaps in the data cannot blur the comparison.

Assumed and written down at registration: the 14-day hold, a daily rule set built inside the method (the monthly fractional Gotrade rules on a daily clock; no preset of that name exists yet), and "regular" meaning 99%-200% of the median of the previous four payments.

## Result against total-return SPY (1996 - Oct 2015, dev window)

On the owner's deposits, SPY with dividends reinvested earned **+7.2% a year**. Every variant lost badly.

| variant | your money per year | worst fall (deposits removed) | gains vs losses | luck check (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ANN-TOEX | +2.0% | 30.7% | 1.09 | 0.10 |
| ANN-THRU | +1.9% | 32.0% | 1.08 | 0.09 |
| ANN-H14 | -0.1% | 48.3% | 1.00 | 0.01 |
| EX-H14 (control) | +0.5% | 61.4% | 1.02 | 0.00 |
| ANN-H14-DEC | -0.3% | 46.8% | 0.99 | 0.01 |
| EX-H14-DEC (control) | +0.4% | 60.2% | 1.02 | 0.00 |

Every variant failed four of the five go-live conditions: it lost to SPY, its worst fall was far over the 20% limit, its gains-vs-losses ratio (winning trades' total over losing trades' total) was about 1.0 against the 1.3 needed, and the **luck check** failed. The luck check (DSR, the deflated Sharpe ratio) asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. The lab now counts N = 56 independent tries, and the bar is 0.90. The best variant scored 0.10.

Walk-forward (picking a variant on past data, then scoring it on years it had not seen) won 1 of 4 folds. Its edge in 2009-2015, the years most like today, was -13.3 points a year.

## Why it lost: the fees eat the book

A window lasts about three weeks, so the book makes roughly **300 stock round trips a year**, and each one also needs a matching SPY sale and purchase. Gotrade charges about 0.2-0.3% of every order plus 11% VAT, with a $0.10 minimum. That is roughly 0.5-0.7% per round trip on each 5% slot, which adds up to **about 8-12% of the whole account a year** in fees. The window premium in the paper is a fraction of a percent per event, so the fees are many times what the window can earn. The gains-vs-losses ratio of almost exactly 1.0 says the same: before fees the windows were slightly positive, and after fees they were nothing.

The falls are mostly the fees too. With deposits removed, EX-H14 lost 7.4% a year through 1996-2001 while SPY made 11.9%. A steady bleed like that turns into a 50-60% "fall" that is not a crash at all.

## The real question: did the announcement date help?

The paired difference (ANN minus EX), month by month with deposits removed, in points a year:

| era | ANN-H14 minus EX-H14 | ANN-H14-DEC minus EX-H14-DEC |
|---|---|---|
| 1996-2015 | +1.3 (t = 1.1) | +1.0 (t = 0.9) |
| 1996-2001 | +5.7 (t = 2.5) | +5.0 (t = 2.2) |
| 2002-2008 | +0.5 (t = 0.3) | +0.8 (t = 0.4) |
| **2009-2015** | **-1.7 (t = -0.9)** | **-2.1 (t = -1.1)** |

The "t" number measures how clearly a difference stands out from month-to-month noise. Around 2 or more is a clear signal; under 1 is noise.

- **Over the whole window the announcement timing gained about 1 point a year, but that is within noise** (t about 1). It also had a smaller worst fall (47-48% against 60-61%), because buying before the ex-date catches the run-up rather than the drop after it.
- **All of that gain came before 2002.** In 1996-2001 it was clear: about 5 points a year. In 2002-2008 it was nothing. In 2009-2015 the announcement timing was **worse** by about 2 points a year. That is not clearly negative, but it is certainly not positive.
- **On the owner's money it was worse.** Measured on the deposits, the announcement versions earned -0.1% and -0.3% a year against +0.5% and +0.4% for the ex-date controls. The deposits pile up over time, so the later years, where the timing hurt, carry the most money.
- The paper's own window (ANN-TOEX) beat the declared-only control by 3.5 points a year (t = 2.9) over the whole period. But it is not a clean pair: it trades less, and it collects every dividend while the control never does. And its 2009-2015 difference was +0.1 points: nothing.

So the plain answer for this batch: **in a short-hold window book, the announcement date did not help in any era that resembles today.** It looks like an edge that existed in the late 1990s and was traded away. That fits the paper being published in 1985, with the lab's 1996-2015 window starting a decade later.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis:** failed. No variant beat SPY, and the announcement arm did not beat the ex-date arm in 2009-2015.
- **Expected failure:** it happened as written, and harder than expected. Fees on a three-week holding period swamped any premium, as they did for the dividend-month book. The book trailed SPY most in 2009-2015 (by 13-15 points a year). The announcement arm caught only a small edge, and only in the early years.

## Comparison with near relatives

The dividend-month book (M0051, monthly, timed from ex-dates) also lost to SPY after fees, by less, because it traded monthly. The dividend-raise book (M0070, held for months) came much closer: +10.9% a year for big raises against SPY's +7.2%. The lesson across all three is that dividend information is only worth something on a slow clock. A raise is a lasting signal that can be held for months; the payment calendar is a short-lived effect that small accounts cannot afford to trade at Gotrade's fees.

**My opinion:** This direction is closed. A three-week dividend window cannot pay for a Gotrade round trip, and the one clear piece of value the announcement date showed (about 5 points a year in 1996-2001) is gone by 2009. No variation of the hold length or the slot count fixes a fee bill near 10% of the account a year. The announcement data is still worth using, but only where it moves a **slow** signal earlier: buying a big dividend raise on the day it is declared instead of weeks later on its ex-date (M0076 in this batch), or selling a holding the day its dividend is cut (M0077). If those also show no announcement-minus-ex-date gain in 2009-2015, the lesson is that the market already prices a declaration within a day, and the data's real use is risk (cuts), not entry timing.
methods.verdict: Rejected: holding stocks from dividend announcement to ex-date lost to SPY by 5-8 points a year; fees on ~300 round trips a year ate the window, and the announcement timing beat ex-date timing only before 2002 (about 2 points worse in 2009-2015)

methods.name: Buy the recovered cutters: big companies six months after a dividend cut, once their price is back above its 200-day average
methods.hypothesis: M0077's cut alarm cost the news-day book about a point a year in 2009-2015 because the big members that cut in 2008-09 later recovered strongly. Test the mirror image: index members whose dividend was cut or omitted 6 to 18 months ago (alarm as M0077, announcement timing) and whose price is now above its own 200-day average, held equal-weight up to 20, rest SPY, behind the SPY-200 switch, monthly, fractional at Gotrade's real fees. Paired control: the same rule timed on the ex-date. Expected failure: about 30 cuts a year among big members leaves the book mostly in SPY outside 2009-2011, so the edge is one episode (the 2009 bank recovery) and the walk-forward folds will be thin; it is also kin of reversal books.

methods.name: Buy a company the week its board declares its first-ever dividend
methods.sourceRef: Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995) JF 50(2): about +7.5% over 12 months after initiations; Asquith & Mullins (1983) JB 56(1); Boehme & Sorescu (2002) JF 57(2) on resumptions; declaration dates from the one-month EODHD pull (2026-10-10)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1983-1995, so the whole dev window is after the crowd could know it. A first dividend is the strongest form of the dividend signal in the papers: a ~3% announcement jump and months of upward drift. M0070 counted initiations only until the company's next payment (about a quarter) and saw them on the ex-date. Here: a point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 member passing F4's $5 price and $20M dollar-volume screen whose dividend is its first in the store (with 400+ days of price history before it) or comes 730+ days after its previous one (a resumption). Held for hold_days from the event date whatever it pays later, up to 10 names at 10% (slots doubled from the idea's 20 x 5% because events are rare: a pre-run count found about 60 first-ever and 30 resumption events among members in 1996-2015, 4-5 a year, bunched in 2003-2004 and 2010-2013), held names first then the newest event, the rest in SPY, behind the SPY-200 switch, fractional at Gotrade's real fees. Paired design, pre-registered: each announced arm (event = declaration date, else the ex-date; declaration lead median 15 days on these events, 86% dated) has an ex-date twin with identical rules, both re-picked weekly so the head start is not wasted (lesson of M0077; weekly-hold-frac-gotrade has no preset, dev only). A-W12/X-W12 hold a year, A-W6/X-W6 six months, A-M12/X-M12 a year on the monthly preset (a promotable twin pair). The quantity of interest is announced minus ex on funded CAGR, worst fall, DSR, 2009-2015 and walk-forward folds. Success for the data: A-W12 beats X-W12 and A-W6 beats X-W6 by half a point a year or more on the deposits. Assumed, not tested: the declared-only pair is dropped (86% dated, so an undated event moves both arms alike); the idea's broader all-store-stocks variant is dropped because the store holds only today's survivors, so a non-member in 1998 is there because it later grew into the index (look-ahead); a one-off special dividend from a non-payer counts as an initiation (no frequency is known then).
methods.expectedFailure: Initiations by index members are rare, so the book is mostly SPY (about 40-60% in stocks at best) and the arms differ on a handful of events: the paired difference may be within noise of zero in either direction. The ~3% announcement jump happens on the declaration day itself, before even the weekly book buys at the next open, so the announced arm gains only the drift between the jump and the ex-date. Initiators are often maturing growth companies (Microsoft 2003, Apple-like tech in 2010-2013): their next year may follow tech, not the dividend. The weekly arms pay more Gotrade fees and churn the SPY-200 switch (M0076's weekly arms fell 32% at worst against 21% monthly), so the weekly variants likely break the 20% worst-fall bar and may lag SPY. A widely published 1990s anomaly: even a real dev edge is likely to fade after 2015. Withholding tax on dividends is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

The papers say the strongest dividend signal is a company paying its **first ever** dividend (or restarting one after years). The price jumps about 3% on the day and then keeps drifting up for months: about +7.5% over a year in the 1995 study. This method bought big index companies (S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members) right after such a dividend, held each for six or twelve months, and kept the rest of the money in SPY. Everything sits in cash while SPY is below its 200-day average.

It is also a test of the dividend announcement dates the owner paid for. Each version was run twice: once seeing the dividend on the day the board **declared** it, and once seeing it only on the **ex-date**, about two weeks later (median 15 days for these events). The difference between the two twins is what the announcement dates are worth.

## How many events there were

Very few. Across 1996-2015 the member universe had **91 such events** (about 60 first-ever, 30 restarts after a 2+ year gap): 8 in 1996-2001, 27 in 2002-2008, 51 in 2009-2015. Most years had 2 to 10. So the book was mostly SPY with a handful of stocks, as expected.

## Results (1996-2015, real Gotrade fees, the owner's monthly top-ups)

| version | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | DSR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-M12 declared, held 1 yr, monthly | +8.1% | +7.2% | 27.8% | 0.81 |
| X-M12 ex-date, held 1 yr, monthly | +8.0% | +7.2% | 29.0% | 0.79 |
| A-W12 declared, held 1 yr, weekly | +3.8% | +7.2% | 31.1% | 0.40 |
| X-W12 ex-date, held 1 yr, weekly | +4.0% | +7.2% | 30.9% | 0.42 |
| A-W6 declared, held 6 mo, weekly | +3.4% | +7.2% | 29.7% | 0.42 |
| X-W6 ex-date, held 6 mo, weekly | +3.2% | +7.2% | 32.8% | 0.41 |

All six are **rejected**. The monthly pair beat SPY by about one point a year but fell 28-29% at its worst, well over the 20% limit. The weekly pairs lost to SPY by more than three points a year and also fell about 30%. DSR is the chance the result is real rather than luck after the lab's N = 53 distinct methods; the bar is 0.90. The best version reached 0.81, so even its small win reads as likely luck.

## Did the announcement dates help?

**No.** Declared minus ex-date, per year on the owner's deposits:

- held a year, weekly: **-0.2 points**
- held six months, weekly: **+0.2 points**
- held a year, monthly: **+0.1 points**

Two of three tiny pluses, one tiny minus, none bigger than a quarter point. The walk-forward check (4 folds, 2003-2014) has the method beating SPY in only 1 of 4. In 2009-2015, the years most like today, the twins are again within half a point of each other (monthly -7.6 vs -7.4 points behind SPY; weekly-1yr -12.3 vs -11.9; weekly-6mo -12.9 vs -13.4).

The event-by-event numbers say why, and they are stronger evidence than the backtest, because they skip the switch and the SPY padding:

- **The declaration-day jump was about zero** for these big companies: +0.4% median, -0.1% mean against SPY. The papers' 3% jump came from small firms in the 1960s-80s, where a first dividend was real news. A big member's first dividend (Microsoft 2003, Cisco 2011, Nvidia 2012) is flagged months ahead by analysts.
- **Between the declaration and the ex-date the stocks drifted -0.1% against SPY** (median -0.6%, 85 dated events). That two-week window is exactly what the earlier timing buys. There was nothing in it.
- Buying on the declaration and holding a year beat buying on the ex-date by +0.4% per event on average, with a spread of 12.6% from event to event. With 86 events that is a standard error of about 1.4%: no signal at all.

## Did the drift itself exist?

Barely, and not where it matters. A year after the declaration these stocks were +4.3% ahead of SPY **on average**, but the **median was -2.0%** and fewer than half (48%) beat SPY. A few big winners carry the mean. The average fades era by era: +17.4% in 1996-2001 (8 events), +4.8% in 2002-2008, +2.0% in 2009-2015 (median -1.7%).

The monthly book's 2002-2008 edge (+9 points a year) is almost all the 200-day switch stepping aside in 2008, not the dividends. M0070's big-raise book, built the same way, had the same 2002-2008 edge with a much smaller fall.

## Why the weekly versions were so much worse

Not the dividends: the **weekly 200-day switch**. Checked every week, SPY's 200-day line whipsaws the book in and out of cash in choppy years (2011 most of all: -21% for the weekly 1-year book, -15% for the monthly one), and each round trip pays Gotrade's fees. M0076's weekly raise book showed the same thing (32% fall weekly against 21% monthly). The lesson from M0077 was "a monthly clock wastes the head start"; this run shows the weekly clock costs far more than any head start is worth, at least with the trend switch on the same clock.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: the declared twins did not beat the ex-date twins by half a point a year. The expected failure happened almost word for word. Events were rare, the book was mostly SPY, the declaration-day jump could not be bought (and for big companies hardly existed), the weekly arms broke the 20% fall limit and lagged SPY, and 2009-2015 lagged SPY in every version. One thing was worse than expected: the 2009-2015 initiators (the tech names that began paying in 2010-2013) were a drag, not just neutral.

## Compared with the near misses

M0070-R25-H6-T (big raises and initiations, monthly, at real fees) did +1.9 / +10.1 / -3.1 points a year against SPY across the three eras. This method did -0.6 / +9.2 / -7.6 for its best version. Taking initiations alone and holding them longer made the book worse in every era. Raises, which are far more common, were carrying M0070, not initiations.

**My opinion:** This direction is finished. First dividends from big index companies do not move their prices the way the papers' small 1970s firms did, and the two weeks the declaration date buys hold no drift to catch. Four methods in this batch now say the same thing about the paid-for dates (M0076, M0077, M0078 and this one): a few tenths of a point either way, never more. I would stop spending ids on "the same rule, timed on the announcement". If the declaration data has any value left, it is as a *filter*, not a clock: for example, how long before the ex-date a board declares (a company that declares early and regularly is a disciplined payer), or whether a raise is announced together with earnings. I'm queuing one idea of that kind. Separately, the weekly-switch finding is worth more than the dividends: any future weekly book should keep its 200-day switch on a monthly clock.
methods.verdict: First-ever dividends from big companies: no real edge over SPY, and seeing them on the declaration day instead of the ex-date changed results by at most 0.2 points a year

methods.name: Disciplined payers: big companies whose board declares the dividend on the same schedule every time
methods.sourceRef: General knowledge: Lintner (1956) dividend smoothing; regular payout policy as a governance signal. Declaration dates from the one-month EODHD pull (2026-10-10). Batch sera-20261010-1742.
methods.hypothesis: Not a published anomaly as such (dividend smoothing is from 1956; the declaration-schedule regularity score is this lab's), so there is no crowd date to fade from, but it sits close to the well-known low-volatility and dividend-quality tilts, which are crowded since ~2012. Four batch tests found the declaration date worthless as an earlier trigger. Use it instead as a quality filter: a board that declares on the same calendar every time, and never cuts, is a company whose cash flow is planned and safe. Among point-in-time S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members passing F4's $5 price and $20M dollar-volume screen with 8+ dividends in the last 3 years, none of the last 8 cut (below 99% of the one before): rank on the spread (days) of the declaration-to-ex lead time over the last 8 payments, all 8 dated. Hold the 20 most regular at 5% (D-N20) or 40 at 2.5% (D-N40), monthly, fractional at Gotrade's real fees, the rest in SPY, behind the SPY-200 switch. Paired control, pre-registered: X-N20 / X-N40 rank on the spread of the gaps between the last 8 ex-dates and read no declaration data, so D minus X is the value of the data as a filter. D-EARLY-N20 asks a second question: among boards with lead spread of 3 days or less, the ones that announce furthest ahead. Success for the data: D beats X by half a point a year or more on funded CAGR at equal or lower worst fall, and holds up in 2009-2015. A pre-run data count (no returns): at mid-2000/2005/2012 about 205-280 qualifying members had all 8 payments dated; the lead spread's 10th percentile is 1.3-2.3 days and median 8-10 days, the ex-gap spread's 10th percentile 0.5 days, with 10-17 exact ties at 0 (ties go to held names, then the symbol). Assumed: a special dividend inside the window counts as a payment and can read as a cut after it (it disqualifies, which is the conservative side); split-adjusted amounts are comparable across a split.
methods.expectedFailure: Regularity mostly marks big, steady, low-volatility payers (utilities, staples, REITs, old industrials): the filter may just re-create the calm-stock book under a new name, and lag SPY in 2009-2015 when growth led. D and X may pick largely the same companies, so the paired difference may be noise. The 20-name book is concentrated in a few sectors, so its worst fall may track utilities/financials (2008 banks were regular payers until they cut). A book of index members equal-weighted leans small next to SPY, the shape every strategy has lost on since 2018. Withholding tax on dividends is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## What was tried

Four earlier methods in this batch (M0076, M0077, M0078, M0081) asked whether the dividend **announcement dates** the owner paid for let the lab act earlier. They did not: a few tenths of a point a year either way. This method asked a different question: is the announcement date useful as a **quality filter** instead of a clock?

The idea: a board that announces each dividend the same number of days before it goes ex, every time, and never cuts it, is a company that plans its cash. Among big index companies (S&P 500 / Nasdaq-100 members, $5+ price, $20M+ a day traded) with at least 8 dividends in the last 3 years and no cut among the last 8, it held the ones whose announcement-to-ex gap varied least (the "D" versions). The rest of the money sat in SPY, and everything went to cash while SPY was below its 200-day average. Monthly, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the owner's monthly top-ups.

The fair comparison was built in: each "D" version had an "X" twin that ranked on how evenly spaced the **ex-dates** were, using no announcement data at all. D minus X is what the paid-for dates add as a filter. A fifth version (D-EARLY) took the steady boards that announce furthest ahead.

## Results (1996-2015, real fees, owner's deposits)

| version | your money per year | SPY, same deposits | worst fall | DSR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-N20: 20 steadiest announcers | +7.7% | +7.2% | 29.7% | 0.80 |
| X-N20: 20 steadiest ex-date spacing | +8.1% | +7.2% | 35.6% | 0.83 |
| D-N40: 40 steadiest announcers | +8.9% | +7.2% | 23.1% | 0.91 |
| X-N40: 40 steadiest ex-date spacing | +9.1% | +7.2% | 27.0% | 0.93 |
| D-EARLY-N20: steady and earliest | +8.0% | +7.2% | 24.2% | 0.82 |

All five are **rejected**. Every one beat SPY over twenty years, by half a point to two points a year, but every one fell more than the 20% limit at its worst (23% to 36%). DSR is the chance the result is real rather than luck after the lab's N = 54 distinct methods; the bar is 0.90. The two 40-name versions cleared it (0.91 and 0.93), the 20-name ones did not.

## Did the announcement dates help as a filter?

**No.** D minus X, per year on the owner's deposits: **-0.4 points** at 20 names and **-0.2 points** at 40. The D versions fell a little less at their worst (29.7% vs 35.6%; 23.1% vs 27.0%), but earned slightly less. Not the half-point win the hypothesis asked for.

The striking part: **the two arms held almost entirely different companies.** At seven dates checked between 1998 and 2015, the 20-name D and X books shared only 0 to 4 stocks. Yet their returns came out within half a point of each other in every era. So the regularity score itself, whichever way it is measured, is picking noise inside a pool. What drives the result is the pool: big companies that have paid 8+ steady, uncut dividends in three years, behind the 200-day switch.

## Where the result came from (book without the deposits, versus SPY)

| era | D-N20 | X-N20 | D-N40 | X-N40 | D-EARLY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1996-2001 | -2.9 | -4.6 | -2.1 | -2.5 | -3.1 |
| 2002-2008 | +7.2 | +10.5 | +9.2 | +9.1 | +8.0 |
| 2009-2015 | -6.4 | -7.5 | -5.6 | -5.0 | -6.3 |

(points a year ahead of or behind SPY with dividends)

- **The whole edge is 2002-2008**, and most of that is the 200-day switch stepping out of the 2008 crash, which every switched book in this lab gets.
- **In 2009-2015, the years most like today, every version lagged SPY by 5 to 7.5 points a year.** That alone rules the direction out (lesson of insight 89/91/93).
- **The worst fall came in 1998-2000, not 2008.** From early 1998 to February 2000 the steady payers drifted down while SPY rose in the dot-com run: the 20-name D book lost about 26% from its peak (book alone, monthly). Steady dividend payers are "old economy" companies, and in a growth-led market they fall behind and even fall outright. The switch does not help there, because SPY was above its 200-day line the whole time.
- Walk-forward (4 folds, 2003-2014): the lab's own choice beat SPY in **1 of 4** folds, and the 2009-2015 edge it reads is -4.9 points. Breadth: every version pays only in "broad" months (when the average stock beats the index) and loses 2-5 points a year in narrow ones, when a few giants carry SPY.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

The hypothesis failed: D did not beat X by half a point, and nothing held up in 2009-2015. The expected failure mostly happened: the book lagged SPY in 2009-2015 when growth led, and D and X differed by noise. One part was wrong: the books were **not** mostly utilities and staples. They were banks, oil majors and industrials (PNC, State Street, Fifth Third, Exxon, Chevron, Emerson, Eaton, 3M, IBM, UPS). That is "old big value", which is exactly why 1998-2000 and 2009-2015 hurt.

## Compared with the near misses

The big-raise book M0070-R25-H6-T (same screen, switch and fees) did +1.9 / +10.1 / -3.1 points a year across the three eras and fell 16.6% at worst. This method did -2.1 / +9.2 / -5.6 at its best (D-N40). A raise is news; a steady schedule is not. M0081's first-dividend book did -0.6 / +9.2 / -7.6. Three dividend books in a row share the same shape: the 2008 switch carries them, and 2009-2015 sinks them.

**My opinion:** This direction is finished, and so, I think, is the paid-for announcement data as a stock picker. Five methods now say the dates add nothing, as a clock or as a filter. The more useful lesson is the pool effect: two books with almost no stocks in common gave the same result, so a ranking inside "steady big dividend payers" is cosmetic, and any dividend-based book here is really a bet on old-economy value against SPY's growth giants. That bet lost in 1998-2000 and 2009-2015 and, by everything the owner's money runs showed, since 2018 too. I would not spend another id on dividend schedules. If the lab tries dividends again, it should be as a small tilt inside a market-shaped book (weighted like SPY, not equally), so the experiment measures the dividend signal and not the value-versus-growth bet.
methods.verdict: Steady dividend schedules: picked almost entirely different stocks from the ex-date control yet earned the same; every version fell 23-36% at worst and lagged SPY by 5-7 points a year in 2009-2015

methods.name: Raises the market cheered: big dividend raises whose stock beat SPY over the two days after the announcement
methods.sourceRef: variation of M0076 (M0070-R25-H6-T's book); Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), JF 50(2); reaction-direction filter after M0063; declaration dates from the one-month EODHD pull (2026-10-10)
methods.hypothesis: Published 1994-1995 (dividend-change drift) and the announcement-reaction literature is older still, so most of the dev window is after the crowd knew both. M0076 showed that seeing a big raise on its declaration day instead of its ex-date adds nothing to the timing (0.3-1.1 points a year worse in all three pairs): the one-day reaction is gone before the next open and the slow drift is caught either way. What the declaration date really carries is the market's reaction to the news. Keep M0070's monthly big-raise book (latest dividend >= 25% over the median of up to four prior payments in 400 days and at most double, or a first payment; up to 20 F4-screened members at 5% while the event is under 182 days old, held names first then the newest event, rest SPY, SPY-200 switch, fractional at Gotrade's real fees) but admit a raise only when its total return beat SPY's over the two sessions starting the event date (close before to close of the next session, dividends in the window added back since closes are not dividend-adjusted; the event waits until that window has closed). Variants, all monthly: A-UP announced and cheered (the idea); X-UP the paired ex-date control, the same filter over the two sessions starting the ex-date, all the old data allowed; A-DN / X-DN the reaction-negative controls; A-UP-D / X-UP-D the up pair counting only dividends that carry a declaration date, so the undated ~13% (whose announced reaction is really an ex-date reaction) cannot blur it. Unfiltered controls already exist: M0076-A-M (+10.3% a year funded) and M0076-X-M (+10.9%). The quantity of interest is A-UP minus X-UP on funded CAGR, worst fall, DSR, 2009-2015 and walk-forward folds, and UP minus DN in each arm. Success for the data: A-UP beats X-UP by a point a year or more and beats A-DN, with the dated pair agreeing in sign.
methods.expectedFailure: The filter roughly halves the set of live raises, so fewer of the 20 slots fill and more of the book sits in SPY; the edge then shrinks toward SPY's whether the filter selects or not. The two-day excess return of a big company is mostly noise (market moves, unrelated news) rather than a verdict on the dividend, so A-UP and A-DN may differ by little; and short-term reversal (M0028) would make a hot two-day start a small negative. The ex-date control may score the same as the announced arm because the drift is slow and either window samples similar noise. M0070's weaknesses carry over: worst fall near the 20% limit (21-22% in fast falls before the SPY-200 switch turns), and lagging SPY in 2009-2015 when big-company growth led. A widely published anomaly from the 1990s: even a real dev edge is likely to fade after 2015. Withholding tax on dividends is not modelled.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-10

## The question

Sera's question for this batch: **does the dividend announcement data help?** M0076 already showed that seeing a big dividend raise on its announcement day, about three weeks before it goes ex, adds nothing to *timing*. This method asks the other thing the announcement date can tell us: **how did the market react?**

The book is M0070's big-raise book, unchanged. It holds up to 20 big index companies whose latest dividend was at least 25% above their usual payment (or a first payment), each at 5% for six months, keeps the rest in SPY, re-picks monthly, and goes to cash while SPY is below its 200-day average. Fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees.

The new rule: a raise only gets in if the stock **beat SPY over the two trading days starting the event day** (from the close the day before to the close of the next day, with any dividend paid in that window added back, because the stored prices are not adjusted for dividends).

## The pairs (all fixed before any result)

- **A** = event day is the announcement day; **X** = event day is the ex-date (all the old data, no announcement dates needed).
- **UP** = only raises the market cheered; **DN** = only raises it shrugged off (the control).
- **-D** = only dividends that carry an announcement date, in both arms, so the 13% without one cannot blur the pair.
- The unfiltered controls already exist: M0076-A-M and M0076-X-M.

## Results (owner's deposits, real fees, 1996-2015; SPY on the same deposits +7.2% a year)

| variant | your money per year | worst fall (with deposits / book alone, monthly) | DSR | 2009-2015 (book alone) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-UP | +9.8% | 19.9% / 15.8% | 0.873 | +12.6% |
| X-UP | +10.6% | 21.1% / 16.0% | 0.918 | +12.5% |
| A-DN | +8.8% | 21.0% / 15.1% | 0.860 | +9.9% |
| X-DN | +8.8% | 25.5% / 18.5% | 0.829 | +11.1% |
| A-UP-D | +9.8% | 21.3% / 15.4% | 0.871 | +12.7% |
| **X-UP-D** | **+10.8%** | **19.9%** / 15.6% | **0.922** | +12.9% |
| *M0076-A-M (no filter)* | +10.3% | 21.3% / 16.1% | 0.932 | +12.4% |
| *M0076-X-M (no filter)* | +10.9% | 21.9% / 16.6% | 0.946 | +13.4% |

SPY alone earned +14.8% a year in 2009-2015. Every variant lagged it there, by 2 to 5 points.

## Announcement minus ex-date (the value of the data)

Paired monthly differences, deposits taken out:

- **UP pair:** announced earned 0.8 points a year less on the deposits (+9.8% vs +10.6%). Monthly, it trailed by 0.047% (t = −0.95), and was ahead in only 7 of 20 years. 2009-2015 was a tie (+12.6% vs +12.5%). The worst fall was a little smaller (19.9% vs 21.1%). DSR was lower (0.873 vs 0.918).
- **Dated-only UP pair:** announced earned 1.0 point a year less (+9.8% vs +10.8%). Monthly: −0.054% (t = −1.09), ahead in 8 of 20 years. 2009-2015 +12.7% vs +12.9%. Worst fall 21.3% vs 19.9%. DSR 0.871 vs 0.922.
- **DN pair:** a dead tie (+8.8% vs +8.8%; t = +0.35).
- **Walk-forward:** the lab's own pick won 2 of 4 folds and changed between folds. It lagged SPY by 3.4 points a year in 2009-2015. Not a majority.

**All three pairs say the same as M0076: the announcement date does not help.** Measuring the market's reaction from the announcement day is no better than measuring it from the ex-date, and slightly worse in both UP pairs. The coverage gap was not hiding anything: the dated-only pair agrees in sign and size.

## Does the reaction filter itself help?

The filter keeps the cheered raises and drops the shrugged-off ones:

- UP beat DN in both arms: by 1.0 point a year on announcement (t = +0.71), and by 1.8 points on ex-date (t = +1.54). Both are suggestive at best, not real evidence.
- **But no UP version beat the unfiltered book.** A-UP earned +9.8% vs +10.3% unfiltered; X-UP earned +10.6% vs +10.9%. The shrugged-off raises *still* earn the drift (+8.8%, well above SPY's +7.2%). Dropping them leaves slots empty for SPY to fill, and SPY earns less than the raises it replaced. So the filter sorts raises slightly, but it costs more than it sorts.
- Exposure was 70% in every variant, same as the unfiltered book. The empty slots go to SPY, so the "invested" share doesn't move; what moves is how much of the book is raises versus SPY.

## The eligible one, read honestly
